(1.4)) = ((ν + 1) k -1)dist(C, F * )
Now, let us describe the high-level ideas of the algorithms for each of the above cases.

Equal Representation with Power-of-Two Colors. When the vertex set V is partitioned into disjoint color groups of equal size, and the total number of colors |χ| is a power of two, we design an algorithm called fairpower-of-two. The algorithm fairpower-of-two constructs a globally fair clustering F fpt by progressively enforcing fairness across larger groups of colors in a hierarchical manner. Starting from an input clustering C defined over a vertex set V , whose points are colored from a color set χ = {c 1 , c 2 , . . . , c d }, the algorithm proceeds in log |χ| iterations:
div.formula: C = N 0 → N 1 → • • • → N log |χ| = F fpt ,
div.p: where N i denotes the clustering obtained after the ith iteration.
In each iteration i, the color set χ is partitioned into contiguous blocks of size 2 i as B i j = {c (j-1)•2 i +1 , c (j-1)•2 i +2 , . . . , c j•2 i }, for j = 1, . . . , |χ|/2 i .
Hence, iteration i enforces local fairness within each block B i j , while later iterations progressively extend this fairness across larger unions of colors.

At the beginning of iteration i, the clustering N i-1 is already locally fair with respect to all blocks of size 2 i-1 . The objective of the current iteration is to produce a new clustering N i such that, for every cluster N i a ∈ N i and for every block B i j , all colors within B i j appear equally in N i a . Formally, for all x, y ∈ {1, . . . , 2 i } with x ̸ = y,
div.formula: c (j-1)•2 i +x (N i a ) = c (j-1)•2 i +y (N i a ),
div.p: where c r (N i a ) denotes the number of points of color c r in cluster N i a . To achieve this, the algorithm first identifies the surplus between each pair of disjoint consecutive blocks within every cluster. For a given cluster N i a and adjacent blocks B i j and B i j+1 for odd j, the surplus T j a is defined as the excess number of points in the larger block relative to the smaller one. Formally, if
div.formula: |B i j (N i a )| > |B i j+1 (N i a )|, then T j a is a subset of B i j (N i a ) of size |B i j (N i a )| -|B i j+1 (N i a )
div.p: |, chosen so that each color in B i j contributes equally to T j a . The definition is symmetric when
div.formula: |B i j+1 (N i a )| > |B i j (N i a )
div.p: |, here B(S) for S ⊆ V and B ⊆ χ denotes the subset of vertices in S that has a color in B.

After identifying these surpluses, the algorithm temporarily removes them from their respective clusters and collects them into two multisets, S j and S j+1 , corresponding to the adjacent blocks B i j and B i j+1 . These two multisets are then passed to the multi-GM subroutine. The multi-GM subroutine is responsible for merging subsets from S j and S j+1 to create new clusters that are locally fair with respect to the union of the two blocks B i j ∪ B i j+1 . It proceeds greedily by pairing subsets of comparable size from the two collections, trimming from the larger subset when necessary, and merging them into balanced clusters. Each resulting cluster thus contains an equal number of points from every color in B i j ∪ B i j+1 . The newly formed fair clusters are then inserted into N i , replacing the previously unbalanced (see Fig. 1.4).

Consequently, each iteration enforces fairness locally across pairs of adjacent color blocks while maintaining at most a factor-2 deviation from the previous clustering. After log |χ| iterations, all colors lie within a single block, and every cluster satisfies global equal representation among all colors. The cumulative approximation factor across all iterations is therefore bounded by

At a high level, the intuition behind the 2-approximation at each step is as follows. For every pair of adjacent color blocks B i 2k-1 and B i 2k , the algorithm first removes the surplus T a 2k-1 from a cluster N i-1 a . This removal incurs a cost of

In the subsequent step, within the multi-gm subroutine, these |T a 2k-1 | surplus points are merged with an equal number of points taken from other clusters. Hence, the total cost incurred by our algorithm for balancing the color blocks
div.formula: (B i 2k-1 , B i 2k ) in the cluster N i-1 a is at most |T a 2k-1 | |N i-1 a | -|T a 2k-1 | + |T a 2k-1 | 2 = |T a 2k-1 | • |N i-1 a |.
div.p: To see that the optimal solution F * must incur a comparable cost, suppose that in F * , the cluster N i-1 a is partitioned into subsets X 1 , X 2 , . . . , X s . (The case s = 1 corresponds to N i-1 a remaining intact in F * .) For the two color blocks B i 2k-1 and B i 2k , we define surpluses S k j ⊆ X j in such a way that
div.formula: s j=1 |S k j | = |T a 2k-1 |.
div.p: The optimal solution must pay a cost of at least
The first term,
div.formula: |S k j | • |N i-1 a \ X j |, accounts for pairs (u, v)
div.p: that were in the same cluster N i-1 a in the input but are separated in F * . The second term, |S k j |•|X j |, captures the merging operation required in F * to restore local fairness within each subcluster X j . The multiplicative factor 1 2 corrects for double counting, since a pair (u, v) with u ∈ S k j and v ∈ S k ℓ (j ̸ = ℓ) would otherwise be counted twice in the summation. To ensure every unordered pair is counted exactly once, we charge each vertex a cost of 1 2 . Thus, even in the optimal solution F * , the minimum possible cost is at least
div.formula: 1 2 |T a 2k-1 | • |N i-1 a |, while our algorithm pays |T a 2k-1 | • |N i-1 a |.
div.p: Hence, the cost of our algorithm is at most twice that of F * , establishing the 2-approximation guarantee for each step.

div.head: Equal Representation with Arbitrary Number of Colors.
div.p: When the vertex set V is partitioned into disjoint color groups of equal size, but the number of colors |χ| is arbitrary (not necessarily a power of two), we design an algorithm called fair-equi. The algorithm fair-equi builds upon two subroutines: fairpower-of-two and make-pdc-fair. The subroutine fairpower-of-two is already described. Let us first describe the high-level idea of make-pdc-fair and then present the construction of fair-equi.

High-Level Idea of make-pdc-fair. The subroutine make-pdc-fair takes as input a clustering I = {I 1 , I 2 , . . . , I η } over a vertex set V whose points are colored from a color set ζ = {z 1 , z 2 , . . . , z r }. The total number of points of each color satisfies a prescribed global proportion

where, without loss of generality, p 1 > p 2 > • • • > p r . Furthermore, each cluster I i in I is assumed to be p-divisible-that is, the number of points of each color z j in I i is an integer multiple of p j .
The goal of make-pdc-fair is to transform I into a clustering F mpf such that every cluster F ∈ F mpf satisfies z 1 (F ) : z 2 (F ) : . . . : z r (F ) = p 1 : p 2 : . . . : p r .

The algorithm proceeds in ⌈log 2 r⌉ iterations, progressively aligning the local color proportions toward the global target ratio. Starting from F 0 := I, it maintains a sequence of refined clusterings
div.formula: I = F 0 → F 1 → • • • → F ⌈log 2 r⌉ = F mpf .
div.p: In each iteration t, make-pdc-fair merges adjacent color blocks in a hierarchical fashion. Initially, each color forms a singleton block B 0 j = {z j }; at every subsequent iteration t ≥ 1, consecutive blocks are merged in pairs:

If the number of blocks m t-1 is odd, the final block remains unpaired and is carried forward unchanged. This process continues until all colors are contained in a single block at iteration T = ⌈log 2 r⌉. At every iteration t, the algorithm ensures that all colors within each block B t i appear in every cluster in proportion to their prescribed global ratios. To achieve this, make-pdc-fair compares the scaling factors of two adjacent blocks B t-1 2i-1 and B t-1 2i within each cluster and tries to equalize the scaling factor. To understand how make-pdc-fair equalizes scaling factors, recall that after iteration (t -1), every cluster F t-1 satisfies the correct color ratios within each block B t-1 2i-1 and B t-1 2i separately. In particular, for
div.formula: B t-1 2i-1 = {z a 1 , . . . , z as } and B t-1 2i = {z b 1 , . . . , z bu },
div.p: we can write the color counts of z a j and z b k for j ∈ [1, s] and k ∈ [1, u] respectively inside F t-1 as
div.formula: z a j (F t-1 ) = p a j • x, z b k (F t-1 ) = p b k • y,
div.p: where the integers x and y are the scaling factors of the two blocks. The values x and y indicate how many times the global ratio vector (p a 1 , . . . , p as ) or (p b 1 , . . . , p bu ) is realized inside the cluster.

.5: Visualization of the make-pdc-fair algorithm for three colors {c 1 , c 2 , c 3 }, with 20, 12, and 8 vertices respectively, corresponding to a global ratio of 5 : 3 : 2. In the first iteration, the color blocks are B 1 1 = {c 1 , c 2 } and B 1 2 = {c 3 }. Hence, in the intermediate clustering F 1 , each cluster maintains the local ratio c 1 : c 2 = 5 : 3. The scaling factor of block B 1 1 in cluster F 1 1 is x = 2, while that of B 1 2 is y = 3. To align these scaling factors, the algorithm cuts 2(y -x) = 2 vertices of color c 3 from F 1 1 and merges them into F 1 2 , yielding the final fair clustering F 2 = F mpf .
When merging these two sub-blocks into a single block
div.formula: B t i = B t-1 2i-1 ∪ B t-1 2i
div.p: , our goal is to make the entire set of colors jointly proportional to their global ratios (p a 1 , . . . , p as , p b 1 , . . . , p bu ). This is possible only if both sub-blocks share the same scaling factor, i.e., x = y. If x ̸ = y, then one group of colors is overrepresented relative to the other.

To correct this imbalance, make-pdc-fair performs a controlled adjustment. Suppose x < y-that is, the sub-block B t-1 2i currently represents the global proportions at a larger scale. The algorithm reduces its contribution by removing p b k • (y -x) points of each color z b k uniformly across the cluster. If x > y then the sub-block B t-1 2i under represents the global proportions. The algorithm increases its contribution by adding p b k • (x -y) points of each color z b k to match the total mass. After this operation, both sub-blocks contribute exactly the same total scaling factor x ′ = y ′ = min(x, y), ensuring that within the combined block B t i , we have z a 1 (F t ) : . . . : z as (F t ) : z b 1 (F t ) : . . . : z bu (F t ) = p a 1 : . . . : p as : p b 1 : . . . : p bu . Since in this setting p a j ≥ p b k for all j ∈ [s] and k ∈ [u], the high-level idea behind the 6approximation at each step of the algorithm make-pdc-fair closely mirrors the reasoning behind the 3-approximation guarantee of the algorithm MakeClustersFair in the two-color case. Recall that MakeClustersFair is the algorithm that transforms a pdc into a fair clustering when the vertex set is divided into two color groups. The additional multiplicative factor of 2 in the approximation bound of make-pdc-fair arises to account for overcounting in the optimal solution, since in the multi-color setting each block may contain multiple colors, and interactions between these colors can lead to double counting of pairwise contributions.

div.head: (see
div.p: High-Level Idea of fair-equi. The algorithm fair-equi takes as input a clustering C whose vertices are colored from χ = {c 1 , c 2 , . . . , c d }, where the colors are distributed equally but |χ| is not a power of two. The key idea is to combine the structural fairness guarantees of fairpower-of-two with the proportional balancing capability of make-pdc-fair.

The algorithm proceeds as follows. First, we partition the color set χ into log |χ| disjoint groups G 1 , G 2 , . . . , G log |χ| such that the size of each group G j is a power of two. This is done greedily according to the binary representation of |χ|: for each index j ∈ [log⌈|χ|⌉], if the corresponding bit in the binary representation of |χ| is 1, a group of size 2 j-1 is created.

Next, fair-equi applies fairpower-of-two independently within each color group G j to obtain an intermediate clustering I = {I 1 , I 2 , . . . , I η } satisfying that for every I i ∈ I and every pair of colors
div.formula: c a , c b ∈ G ℓ , c a (I i ) = c b (I i ).
div.p: Thus, fairpower-of-two ensures equal representation within each power-of-two-sized color group.

We then treat each group G ℓ as a single meta-color z ℓ ∈ ζ and invoke the make-pdc-fair subroutine on the intermediate clustering I. The clustering I serves as a p-divisible clustering because for each cluster I i ∈ I, the count |G ℓ (I i )| is divisible by |G ℓ |, where G ℓ (I i ) denotes the subset of vertices of I i that has a color from the group G ℓ . Applying make-pdc-fair produces a final fair clustering F = {F 1 , . . . , F ι } such that for every cluster F j ∈ F,

Since fairpower-of-two already enforces equality within each group G ℓ , the proportional balancing across groups performed by make-pdc-fair ensures that in the final clustering F , every color c u , c v ∈ χ satisfies c u (F j ) = c v (F j ). Thus, fair-equi outputs a globally fair clustering where all colors are equally represented in every cluster.

As established earlier, the algorithm fairpower-of-two achieves an approximation factor of O(|χ| 1.6 ). In the algorithm fair-equi, the number of meta-colors generated is at most log |χ|, and consequently, the subroutine make-pdc-fair contributes an additional approximation factor of O(log 2.81 |χ|). By applying the triangle inequality to combine the errors introduced by the two stages, the overall approximation factor of fair-equi becomes O(|χ| 1.6 log 2.81 |χ|).

div.head: Arbitrary Representation.
div.p: When the vertex set V is divided into disjoint color groups of arbitrary sizes, we design an algorithm fair-general to construct a fair clustering that reflects the global color distribution. Let the vertices be colored from the set χ = {c 1 , c 2 , . . . , c d }, and suppose their total counts satisfy the global ratio
To achieve fairness under these non-uniform proportions, we adopt a two-step approach analogous to the two-color case.

In the first step, we construct a p-divisible clustering (pdc) M = {M 1 , M 2 , . . . , M t } using our algorithm create-pdc. Recall in a pdc M, for every cluster M ∈ M and every color c j ∈ χ, the number of points of color c j in M is divisible by p j .
In the second step, we transform the p-divisible clustering M into a fair clustering F using make-pdc-fair such that for every cluster F ∈ F ,

High level idea of create-pdc: To construct a pdc, we proceed iteratively over the colors in χ. For each color c j , we apply the algorithm AlgoforGeneral introduced in the two-color case. At iteration j, the algorithm AlgoforGeneral is applied to the current clustering to ensure that, within every cluster, the number of vertices of color c j becomes a multiple of p j . Thus, after processing all colors sequentially, in the resulting clustering for all colors c j the number of vertices of color c j is divisible by p j .

Recall that in the two-color setting, the algorithm AlgoforGeneral takes as input a clustering whose vertices are divided into two color groups-say blue and red-such that the global ratio of blue to red points is p : 1. The output of AlgoforGeneral is a refined clustering where, in every cluster, the number of blue vertices is a multiple of p. By applying this procedure iteratively to each color c j , we generalize the same principle to the multi-color setting, thereby obtaining a pdc.

As discussed earlier, the algorithm AlgoforGeneral achieves an approximation factor of 3.5 in the two-color setting. When AlgoforGeneral is applied iteratively across all colors in χ, these approximation factors accumulate, resulting in an overall approximation factor of O(|χ|) for the algorithm create-pdc. It is worth noting that if one were to apply a direct analysis using the triangle inequality, a constant-factor approximation ν at each step would compound multiplicatively, yielding an overall factor of ν |χ| . To avoid this exponential blow-up, we adopt a refined analytical approach inspired by Chakraborty et al. [CCD + 25], originally developed for the two-color setting where the blue-to-red ratio is an arbitrary p : q. This sophisticated analysis allows us to bound the cumulative approximation additively rather than multiplicatively, thereby ensuring an O(|χ|) guarantee for create-pdc.

High-Level Idea of fair-general: Given an input clustering C, the algorithm fair-general proceeds in two stages. First, it applies create-pdc to construct a pdc clustering M, ensuring that within each cluster, the number of points of color c j is divisible by p j . Subsequently, it invokes make-pdc-fair on M to produce the final fair clustering F.

The algorithm create-pdc achieves an approximation factor of O(|χ|), while make-pdc-fair contributes an additional factor of O(|χ| 2.81 ). Combining these guarantees, fair-general attains an overall approximation factor of O(|χ| 3.81 ).

div.head: Fair Consensus Clustering in the Streaming Setting
div.p: In fair consensus clustering, the input consists of a collection of clusterings I = {C 1 , . . . , C m } defined on a common vertex set. The objective is to compute a fair clustering F such that
div.formula: m i=1 dist(C i , F) ℓ 1/ℓ ≤ (α + 1.995) m i=1 dist(C i , F * con ) ℓ 1/ℓ ,
div.p: where F * con denotes an optimal fair consensus clustering, and α, ℓ are fixed parameters. We assume oracle access to an α-approximate closest fair clustering algorithm. Our goal is to compute such a clustering F using only O(n log m) space and O n 2 log 4 m + t 1 (n) log 3 m time, where t 1 (n) denotes the running time of an unweighted fair correlation clustering algorithm.
We work in the streaming model pairwise streaming model described in Section 1.1. We now describe our streaming algorithm, denoted by algo-fair-con-stream.

High-Level Idea of algo-fair-con-stream: Recall that in the pairwise consensus streaming model, each stream element is a triple (p, j, b) that encodes information about the j-th clustering C j ∈ I. Prior to processing the stream, we uniformly sample 4g log m indices j 1 , . . . , j 4g log m from [m], for a suitable constant g > 1, and store only the information corresponding to the sampled clusterings C j 1 , . . . , C j 4g log m .

Using these sampled clusterings, we construct a candidate set of fair clusterings, denoted by F. The key guarantee is that, with high probability, F contains at least one fair clustering F that achieves an (α + 1.995)-approximation to the optimal fair consensus clustering. Accordingly, we output the clustering
div.formula: F = arg min F ′ ∈ F m i=1 dist(C i , F ′ ) ℓ 1/ℓ .
div.p: A key technical challenge in our setting is evaluating the objective value of a candidate clustering F ′ ∈ F. In the streaming model, computing its distance to all input clusterings C i ∈ I is infeasible, since only O(log m) clusterings can be stored at any time. To overcome this limitation, we leverage a result due to Indyk [Ind99; Ind01]. Specifically, if we uniformly sample a subset W ⊆ I of size Ω(ε -2 log m), for any 0 < ε < 1, then with probability at least 1 -1/m, the following guarantee holds:
div.formula: m i=1 dist(C i , F best,W ) ℓ 1/ℓ ≤ (1 + ε) m i=1 dist(C i , F best,I ) ℓ 1/ℓ .
div.p: Here, F best,W denotes the fair clustering in F that minimizes the objective when evaluated only on the sampled set W, while F best,I denotes the fair clustering in F that minimizes the objective when evaluated over the full set I.

We therefore independently sample an additional 64ε -2 log m clusterings from I to form the set W, and use W to approximately evaluate the objective function for all candidates in F. Since we store only O(log m) clusterings in total, and each clustering requires O(n) space, the overall space complexity of the algorithm is O(n log m). To analyze the approximation factor and the time complexity of the algorithm, we need to look at the construction of F.

Construction of the Candidate Set F : After sampling 4g log m input clusterings, for each sampled clustering C k (where k ∈ [4g log m]), we compute and store its α-close fair clustering F C k in the candidate set F. In addition, for every triple (C x , C y , C z ) of sampled clusterings, we perform the following steps.

(i) We construct an unweighted correlation clustering instance G x,y,z from the three clusterings C x , C y , and C z . For each unordered vertex pair (u, v), the edge (u, v) in G x,y,z is assigned a positive label if u and v are placed in the same cluster in at least two of the three clusterings; otherwise, the edge is assigned a negative label.
(ii) We compute an unweighted fair correlation clustering T x,y,z on the graph G x,y,z using a known algorithm for unweighted fair correlation clustering.
(iii) We add the clustering T x,y,z to the candidate set F.
We refer to the above procedure as the cluster fitting algorithm, denoted by ClusterFitting. We now provide intuition for why the ClusterFitting algorithm is effective.

div.head: Let F *
div.p: con denote an optimal fair consensus clustering. For each input clustering C i ∈ I, let I i denote the set of unordered vertex pairs (u, v) ∈ V × V such that u and v are clustered together (respectively, separated) in F * con , but are separated (respectively, clustered together) in C i . By definition, dist(C i , F * con ) = |I i |. We further define
div.formula: OPT = m i=1 dist(C i , F * con ) ℓ 1/ℓ
div.p: and AVG = OPT m .
It can be shown that if at least m/g input clusterings are close to the optimal solution F * con , that is, if there exists a set of at least m/g indices such that
div.formula: |I i | ≤ (1 -β)AVG
div.p: for some parameter β > 1, then with high probability our sampling procedure selects one such clustering C i . In this case, the corresponding α-close fair clustering F C i yields an (α + 1.995)approximation to the optimal fair consensus clustering.

The more challenging case arises when fewer than m/g clusterings are close to F * con . In this regime, the ClusterFitting algorithm becomes crucial. Specifically, consider triples (C x , C y , C z ) for which each of |I x |, |I y |, and |I z | is large-exceeding (1 -β)AVG-but whose pairwise intersections are bounded. That is, for all distinct r, s ∈ {x, y, z},
div.formula: |I r ∩ I s | ≤ α AVG.
div.p: For such triples, the fair clustering T x,y,z produced by the ClusterFitting algorithm is close to the optimal solution F * con , and consequently achieves an (α + 1.995)-approximation. The intuition underlying why the clustering T x,y,z is close to F * con is as follows. Consider a vertex pair (u, v) ∈ I r ∩I s for some distinct indices r, s ∈ {x, y, z}. Without loss of generality, assume that u and v are clustered together in C r and C s . Since (u, v) ∈ I r ∩ I s , it follows that u and v are separated in the optimal fair consensus clustering F * con . By construction of the correlation clustering instance G x,y,z , the edge (u, v) receives a positive label whenever u and v are clustered together in at least two of the three clusterings C x , C y , and C z . Therefore, for the pair (u, v) under consideration, the edge (u, v) is labeled positive in G x,y,z . Consequently, in the unweighted fair correlation clustering T x,y,z computed from G x,y,z , vertices u and v are placed in the same cluster.

When comparing T x,y,z to the optimal clustering F * con , the clustering T x,y,z incurs a cost for the pair (u, v), since u and v are clustered together in T x,y,z but separated in F * con . Thus, every pair belonging to the intersection I r ∩ I s necessarily contributes to the disagreement between T x,y,z and F * con . Therefore, if the total number of such pairs is bounded, the overall disagreement between T x,y,z and F * con is small, implying that T x,y,z is close to F * con . We show that, with high probability, our sampling procedure selects clusterings C x , C y , and C z whose corresponding pairwise intersections are bounded. Consequently, with high probability, the algorithm achieves an approximation factor of (α + 1.995).

We now analyze the running time of the algorithm. The candidate set F contains O(log 3 m) clusterings. The dominating cost to construct these candidates is by applying the ClusterFitting procedure to all triples of sampled clusterings which requires O t 1 (n) log 3 m time.

To select the best clustering from F, we evaluate the objective function for each candidate. This requires O(log 3 m) evaluations. In each evaluation, we compute the distance between the candidate clustering and each clustering in the sampled set W. Computing the distance between two clusterings takes O(n 2 ) time, and since |W| = O(log m), the total time per evaluation is O(n 2 log m). Therefore, the total time required for all evaluations is O(n 2 log 4 m).
Combining these bounds, the overall running time of the algorithm is
div.formula: O n 2 log 4 m + t 1 (n) log 3 m .

div.head: Organization
div.p: The remainder of this thesis is organized as follows. In Chapter 2, we present our results on faulttolerant reachability preservers. The Chapter 3 studies the closest fair clustering problem when the vertex set V is partitioned into two disjoint color groups, while Chapter 4 extends these results to settings with more than two color groups. In Chapter 5, we explore the implications of our closest fair clustering framework for fair correlation clustering and fair consensus clustering. The Chapter 6 presents our algorithmic results for fair consensus clustering in the streaming setting.
Finally, Chapter 7 outlines several open problems and directions for future research.

div.head: Reachability Preservers
div.p: In this chapter, we present a construction of a dual fault-tolerant reachability preserver (2-FTRS) for a given directed graph G = (V, E) and a vertex-pair set P ⊆ V × V . Specifically, we establish Theorem 1, which we restate below.

div.head: Theorem 1 (Upper Bound on 2-FTRS).
div.p: For any directed graph G = (V, E) with n vertices and a set P ⊆ V × V of vertex-pairs, there exists a 2-FTRS(G, P) having at most O(n 4/3 |P| 1/3 ) edges. Furthermore, we can find such a subgraph in polynomial time.

To prove this result, we first describe an alternate construction of a 2-FTRS for a single vertex pair. We then extend this construction to handle multiple pairs, thereby obtaining the general result.

div.head: An (Alternate) Construction of 2-FTRS for a Single Pair
div.p: Given any directed graph G with n vertices, for any pair of vertices (s, t), we already get an O(n) size 2-FTRS(G, (s, t)) from [BCR16]. Let us state the result of [BCR16] formally here.

div.head: Theorem 12 ([BCR16]).
div.p: For any directed graph G = (V, E), a designated source vertex s ∈ V , and an integer k ≥ 1, there exists a (sparse) subgraph H of G which is a k-FTRS(G, {s} × V ) and contains at most 2 k n edges. Moreover, such a subgraph is computable in O(2 k mn) time, where n and m are respectively the number of vertices and edges in graph G.

However, now we study the structure of a 2-FTRS(G, (s, t)) more closely and provide a slightly different construction which will be useful for our construction of 2-FTRS for multiple pairs. Let us first define a notation to denote the ordering of vertices on a specific path. For any path P and two vertices u, v on P , we will write u < P v if and only if u appears before v on P .
Suppose we are given a directed graph G and a pair (s, t). Let us consider two s -t paths P 1 (s,t)

and P 2 (s,t) , that intersect only at s -t cut-edges and s -t cut-vertices. We call these two paths outer strands. Next, we define coupling paths between these two outer strands. For each vertex on the outer strands, let us first define two coupling points of it (one on each outer strand). Consider a vertex v ∈ V (P 1 (s,t) ∪ P 2 (s,t) ) and i ∈ {1, 2} where for a subgraph H of G, V (H) represents the set of vertices in the graph H. Then consider the vertex u i (s,t),v ∈ P i (s,t) (if exists) for which there is a u i (s,t),v -v path that is edge-disjoint with both the outer strands, and there is no vertex u ′ ∈ P i (s,t)

such that u ′ < P i (s,t) u i (s,t),v and there is a u ′ -v path that is edge-disjoint with both the outer strands. We refer to u 1 (s,t),v , u 2 (s,t),v as coupling points of v. For each v on the outer strands and each coupling point u i (s,t),v of it, consider any arbitrary u i (s,t),v -v path (denoted as Q i (s,t),v ) of G, that is edge-disjoint with both the outer strands. We refer to the path Q i (s,t),v as a coupling path to v. Note, for each vertex v on the outer strands, there are at most two coupling points of it (one on each outer strand) and from each coupling point there is a coupling path to v. We take two outer strands and some of the coupling paths to build a subgraph H (s,t) . More specifically, for a vertex v ∈ V (P j (s,t) ), if for all the vertices below v on that strand, their coupling points on a strand P i (s,t)

is below the coupling point of v on that strand, then only add the coupling path from the strand P i (s,t) to v. Later, we prove that keeping these "essential" coupling paths is sufficient. Below we provide a formal description of the procedure to construct H (s,t) . Given G and a pair (s, t), we build a subgraph H (s,t) as follows:
2. Add all the edges on the paths P 1 (s,t) , P 2 (s,t) (two outer strands) to H (s,t) .
3. For all i, j ∈ {1, 2} and v ∈ V (P j (s,t) )
div.formula: (a) If for all v ′ ∈ V (P j (s,t) [v -t]), u i (s,t),v < P i (s,t) u i
div.p: (s,t),v ′ , then take the coupling path Q i (s,t),v , and add all its edges to H (s,t) . Here. P j (s,t) [v -t] denotes the subpath of P j (s,t) from v to t.
Readers may refer to Figure 1.1 for an example subgraph H (s,t) . Note, the above construction procedure of the subgraph H (s,t) runs in polynomial time.

Before arguing that H (s,t) is a 2-FTRS(G, (s, t)), let us introduce a notion of nice path. We call an s -t path in H (s,t) nice if it first follows a outer strand till some vertex u, then take a coupling path to some vertex u ′ , and finally follows the outer strand on which u ′ lies till t. To state it formally, suppose for two paths P and Q, P • Q denotes the concatenation of two paths P and Q. Now, an s -t path in H (s,t) is nice if and only if it is of the form P i (s,t) [s -u] • Q i (s,t),u ′ • P j (s,t) [u ′ -t], for some i, j ∈ {1, 2}, where subpath Q i (s,t),u ′ starts from u and is edge-disjoint with both the outer strands P 1 (s,t) , P 2 (s,t) . (Q i (s,t),u ′ could be empty.) The following claim shows that H (s,t) is a 2-FTRS(G, (s, t)), and also will be useful in the next subsection while arguing about the correctness of our pairwise 2-FTRS for multiple pairs construction.
Claim 2.1.1. For any two edges f 1 , f 2 , if there is an s -t path in G \ {f 1 , f 2 }, then there must be a nice s -t path in H (s,t) \ {f 1 , f 2 }.
Proof. First of all, one of f 1 , f 2 must be on P

1 (s,t) and another on P 2 (s,t) . Otherwise, since P 1 (s,t) and P 2 (s,t) intersect only at s-t cut-edges and s-t cut-vertices, at least one of P 1 (s,t) , P 2 (s,t) remains intact in H (s,t) \ {f 1 , f 2 }, and thus there is nothing to prove. So from now on without loss of generality, assume, f 1 = (x 1 , y 1 ) lies on P 1 (s,t) and f 2 = (x 2 , y 2 ) lies on P 2 (s,t) . Let P be an s-t path in G\{f 1 , f 2 }. Observe, P must intersect either P 1 (s,t) [y 1 -t] or P 2 (s,t) [y 2 -t]. Let z ′ be the first vertex on P , that is also in V (P 1 (s,t) [y 1 -t] ∪ P 2 (s,t) [y 2 -t]) (such a vertex exists because P , P 1 (s,t) and P 2 (s,t) all end at t). Let z ′ lie on P j (s,t) , for some j ∈ {1, 2}. Now consider the last vertex before z ′ on P , that is also in V (P 1 (s,t) ∪ P 2 (s,t) ) (such a vertex exists because P , P 1 (s,t) and P 2 (s,t) all start from s), and let z be that vertex which is on P i (s,t) , for some i ∈ {1, 2}. (i could be equal to j.) Observe, z must lie on the subpath P i (s,t) [s -x i ]. Furthermore, P [z -z ′ ] is edge-disjoint with P 1 (s,t) and P 2 (s,t) . Hence, by the construction of H (s,t) , there must be a path Q i (s,t),u ′ for some u ′ ∈ V (P j (s,t) [z ′ -t]) which starts from a vertex u < P i (s,t) z < P i (s,t) x i (u could be equal to z). Hence, P i (s,t) [s -u] remains intact in H (s,t) \ {f 1 , f 2 }. Note, u ′ ∈ V (P j (s,t) [y j -t] (because u ′ ∈ V (P j (s,t) [z ′ -t])). Thus the subpath P j (s,t) [u ′ -t] also remains intact in H (s,t) \ {f 1 , f 2 }. Lastly, since Q i (s,t),u ′ is edge-disjoint with P 1 (s,t) and P 2 (s,t) , it also remains intact in H (s,t) \ {f 1 , f 2 }. Hence, we get an s -t path P i (s,t)
div.formula: [s -u] • Q i (s,t),u ′ • P j (s,t) [u ′ -t] in H (s,t) \ {f 1 , f 2 }.
div.p: Next, let us use the above claim to conclude that H (s,t) is a 2-FTRS(G, (s, t)). Furthermore, we also argue that the size of H (s,t) is O(n).
Lemma 2.1.2. H (s,t) is a 2-FTRS(G, (s, t)) and contains O(n) edges.

Proof. Since H (s,t) is a subgraph of G, from Claim 2.1.1, we conclude that for any two edges f 1 , f 2 , there is an s -t path in G \ {f 1 , f 2 } if and only if there is an s -t path in H (s,t) \ {f 1 , f 2 }. So, H (s,t) is a 2-FTRS(G, (s, t)).
Let us now compute the size of H (s,t) . First, we would like to claim that for each vertex
div.formula: v ∈ V (H (s,t) ) \ V (P 1 (s,t) ∪ P 2 (s,t) ), in-degree of v in H (s,t) is at most 4. If not, then there exists a vertex v ∈ V (H (s,t) ) \ V (P 1 (s,t) ∪ P 2 (s,t) )
div.p: with at least five incoming edges e 1 , e 2 , e 3 , e 4 , e 5 . Suppose during the construction of H (s,t) , for each r ∈ [5], e r has been included while adding a path Q ir (s,t),vr , where v r ∈ V (P jr (s,t) ). Since for each r ∈ [5], i r , j r ∈ {1, 2}, by the pigeonhole principle, there must exist r ̸ = r ′ ∈ [5] such that i r = i r ′ (= i) and j r = j r ′ (= j). Without loss of generality, assume, v r < P j s,t v r ′ . Since Q i (s,t),vr and Q i (s,t),v r ′ intersect at v, either u i (s,t),v r ′ = u i (s,t),vr or u i (s,t),v r ′ < P i (s,t) u i (s,t),vr . Hence, by the Step 3(a) of the construction procedure of H (s,t) , Q ir (s,t),vr would not be added, which leads to a contradiction.
Observe, by the construction of H (s,t) , in-degree of each v ∈ V (P 1 (s,t) ∪ P 2 (s,t) ) is also at most 4. Hence, H (s,t) has total O(n) edges.

div.head: Dual Fault-tolerant Pairwise Reachability Preserver
div.p: In this section, we provide the construction of 2-FTRS for multiple pairs, and thus prove Theorem 1. To prove Theorem 1 we provide a construction of 2-FTRS with slack. Let us define it below.

div.head: Sparsifiers with Slack.
div.p: In case of pairwise FTRS we want to construct an subgraph that provides correct reachability information for all the given vertex-pairs even after edge failures. This is the most standard definition of pairwise FTRS. Next, we define a variant which we refer to as pairwise FTRS with slack. Interested readers may find more works on sparsifiers with slack in [CDG06; KRX + 07; Din07; Bod22]. Given a graph G and a pair set P, a subgraph H is a k-FTRS with slack if there is P ′ ⊆ P, |P ′ | = Ω(|P|) such that H is a k-FTRS for the pair set P ′ .
The following lemma from [Bod22] shows that to construct a k-FTRS for a pair set, it suffices to construct a k-FTRS with slack.
Lemma 2.2.1 ( [Bod22]). Let us consider constants α, β, γ > 0 and a parameter p * . Consider a graph G(V, E) with n vertices. If
• There is a k-FTRS of size O(n α ) for any vertex-pair set P of size at most p * , and

• There is a k-FTRS with slack of size O(n β |P| γ ) for any vertex-pair set P of size at least p * , then there is a k-FTRS(G, P) of size at most O(n α + n β |P| γ ). Moreover, if the k-FTRS for at most p * pairs and the k-FTRS with slack for at least p * pairs can be computed in polynomial time, then the k-FTRS(G, P) can also be computed in polynomial time.
Thus, due to Lemma 2.2.1 to prove Theorem 1 it suffices to construct 2-FTRS with slack. To construct that, we need the concept of fractional hitting set.

Fractional Hitting Set. Let U := {1, 2, • • • , n} be the universe. A set S ⊆ U is said to be a hitting set of a family of subsets S 1 , S 2 , • • • , S m ⊆ U if and only if for all i ∈ [m], S ∩ S i ̸ = ∅ (i.e., S intersects all the subsets S i ). Given a family of subsets, the problem of finding the minimum sized hitting set is referred to the hitting set problem, and is known to be NP-complete. However, there is a simple greedy algorithm that given any family of subsets S 1 , • • • , S m each of size at least k, finds a hitting set of size at most O( n k log n). In this thesis, we consider a variant of the hitting set problem, which we call fractional hitting set. A set S ⊆ U is said to be a hitting set with slack of a family of subsets S 1 , • • • , S m if and only if |{i ∈ [m] | S ∩ S i ̸ = ∅}| = Ω(m) (i.e., S has a non-empty intersection with at least a constant fraction of the input subsets). It is not difficult to see that the above mentioned greedy hitting set algorithm finds a fractional hitting set of size at most O(n/k).

Theorem 13. There is a deterministic algorithm that given a family of subsets S 1 , • • • , S m ⊆ [n] each of size at least k, finds a fractional hitting set of size at most O(n/k) in time O(n+mk+ n k log n). Proof. W.l.o.g. assume, each S i is of size exactly k; otherwise we can just consider any k elements from each S i . Let us now consider a slightly modified version of the standard greedy algorithm for the hitting set problem. Initialize F := {S 1 , • • • , S m }, and S = ∅. For each v ∈ [n], compute the number of subsets in F that contains v, i.e., c(v) := |{S i ∈ F | v ∈ S i }|. Let v max be a maximizer of c(v). Include v max in S, i.e, S ← S ∪ {v max }. Remove all the subsets that contains v max from F, i.e., F ← F \ {S i | v max ∈ S i }. Continue this process R = 4n/k times, and output S. (Note, instead to continuing the process until F = ∅ as in the standard greedy algorithm for the hitting set problem, we terminate after a fixed number of steps.)

Clearly, |S| = R = O(n/k). We would like to claim that S is a fractional hitting set. For that purpose, it suffices to show that at the end of the algorithm |F | ≤ m/10. Let n j denote the size of F after the j-th element is added in S. n 0 = m, and we need to show that n R ≤ m/10. Consider the step when the j-th element has been added in S. Observe, v∈[n]\H c(v) = n j-1 k, and thus by a simple averaging, an element v j max that maximizes c(v) must satisfy c(v j max ) ≥ n j-1 k n-j+1 . Thus,
div.formula: n j ≤ 1 - k n -j + 1 n j-1 ≤ m j-1 r=0 1 - k n -r < m(1 -k/n) j ≤ me -kj/n .
div.p: Then for R = 4n/k, n R < m/10. The running time of the modified algorithm is bounded by the standard greedy algorithm for the hitting set problem. For the sake of completeness, let us briefly comment on the running time analysis. At the beginning we can compute the values of c(v)'s, and then store them using any standard heap data structure (e.g. [BLT12]). Then at each step, we extract the max value, and then we update the values of the others. This gives the total time to be O(n + mk + n k log n). Theorem 14. For any directed graph G = (V, E) with n vertices and a set P ⊆ V × V of vertexpairs, there exists a 2-FTRS with slack having at most O(n 4/3 |P| 1/3 ) edges. Furthermore, we can find such a subgraph in polynomial time.
Now we are ready to describe the construction of 2-FTRS with slack. We will use the notations H (s,t) , P i (s,t) , Q j (s,t),v defined in Section 2.1. Apart from them, we need a few more notations.
• freq B (v) denotes the frequency of a vertex in a set of paths B, more elaborately, for any set B of paths in G, for any vertex v ∈ V , freq B (v) denotes the number of paths in B that contains v.
• P [L] : The subpath of the path P containing the first L vertices of P .
• P [-L] : The subpath of the path P containing the last L vertices of P .
Procedure to Construct a 2-FTRS with slack for the input (G, P):

1. For each (s, t) ∈ P, construct H (s,t) = 2-FTRS(G, (s, t)) using the construction provided in Section 2.1. (Recall, H (s,t) contains two s -t paths P 1 (s,t) and P 2 (s,t) , that intersect only at s -t cut-edges and s -t cut-vertices.) Define H inter = (s,t)∈P H (s,t) .

2. Consider the following family of subsets F := {V (P i (s,t) 5. Let B be the set of all the paths Q i (s,t),v (defined in Section 2.1) for (s, t) ∈ Q, v ∈ V (∪ j∈{1,2} P j (s,t) [-L]) and i ∈ {1, 2}. 6. Initialize an empty set W . 7. While ∃v ∈ V such that freq B (v) ≥ L|Q| (a) Add v to W and remove all the paths that contains v from B. 8. For each w ∈ W , construct a 2-FTRS(G, {w} × V ) and 2-FTRS(G, V × {w}), and take union of all these subgraphs to get a subgraph H 3 . 9. Let H 4 be the subgraph obtained by taking the union of all the (remaining) paths in B. Again, we use Theorem 12 to build a 2-FTRS(G, {w} × V ) and 2-FTRS(G, V × {w}) for each w ∈ W . Thus the size of H 3 is at most O(n L|Q|).

Since H 4 is the union of all the leftover paths in B after the while loop, in-degree of each vertex in H 4 is at most L|Q|. So the size of H 4 is O(n L|Q|). Hence, we conclude that the size of the final subgraph H is O((n|P|

Correctness of pairwise 2-FTRS with slack. Next, we would like to claim that the subgraph H is a 2-FTRS with slack for (G, P). First, we show that the constructed data structure is a 2-FTRS(G, Q). Second, we show that |Q| = Ω(|P|). The second part is quite straightforward. By the definition of fractional hitting set, S intersects all but 1/10 fraction of the subsets of F. Hence, |Q| ≥ 3 5 |P|. So it only remains to show the first part.
Lemma 2.2.2. The subgraph H is a 2-FTRS(G, Q).

Proof. Consider any arbitrary pair (s, t) ∈ Q. It is immediate from the definition of a 2-FTRS that any 2-FTRS(H (s,t) , (s, t)) is also a 2-FTRS(G, (s, t)). So to prove Lemma 2.2.2, it suffices to show that for all (s, t) ∈ Q, H is a 2-FTRS(H (s,t) , (s, t)). From now on we will focus on proving this latter claim. Suppose there is an s -t path in H (s,t) \ {f 1 , f 2 }. Observe, by Claim 2.1.1, there must be a nice s -t path R in H (s,t) \ {f 1 , f 2 }. By the definition of nice path, R would be of the form
div.formula: P i (s,t) [s -u] • Q i(
div.p: s,t),u ′ • P j (s,t) [u ′ -t], for some i, j ∈ {1, 2}, where the subpath Q i (s,t),u ′ starts from the vertex u and is edge-disjoint with P 1 (s,t) and P 2 (s,t) . (Q i (s,t),u ′ could be empty; in that case, R = P i (s,t) for some i ∈ {1, 2}.) By the definition of Q, P i (s,t) [L] ∩ S ̸ = ∅ and P j (s,t) [-L] ∩ S ̸ = ∅. Now, if u does not lie on P i (s,t) [L], i.e., the length of the subpath P i (s,t) [s -u] is at least L, then R must pass through a vertex v ∈ P i (s,t) [L] ∩ S. Similarly, if u ′ does not lie on P j (s,t) [-L], then R must pass through a vertex v ∈ P j (s,t) [-L] ∩ S. In both the scenarios, for some v ∈ S, there is an s -v and v -t path in H (s,t) \ {f 1 , f 2 } (and thus also in G \ {f 1 , f 2 }). This means, by the construction of
div.formula: H 1 (Step 3), there is an s -v and v -t path in H 1 \ {f 1 , f 2 } as well.
div.p: So let us now focus on the case when u lies on P i (s,t) Let us now combine Theorem 14 with Lemma 2.2.1 to finish the proof of Theorem 1.

Proof of Theorem 1. For single pair, by [BCR16], we have a 2-FTRS of size O(n) that can be computed in polynomial time. By Theorem 14, we have a 2-FTRS with slack of size O(n 4/3 |P| 1/3 ). Theorem now directly follows from Lemma 2.2.1.

div.head: Closest Fair Clustering with Two Colors
div.p: In this chapter, we present an algorithm to construct a fair clustering F which is 17-close to an input clustering C, when the irreducible ratio of blue to red vertices is p : 1 for some integer p > 1. More specifically, we prove Theorem 4, which we restate below.

Theorem 4. Let the vertex set V be partitioned into two disjoint groups, blue and red, where the ratio of blue to red vertices in V is p : 1 for some integer p > 1. Then there exists a polynomial-time algorithm that computes a 17-close fair clustering with respect to a given input clustering C.
Our approach proceeds in two stages. In the first stage, given an input clustering C, we compute a p-divisible clustering T . In the second stage, we take T as input and produce a fair clustering F.
Definition 3.0.1 (p-Divisible Clustering). Let V be a set of vertices colored from the set χ = {c 1 , . . . , c r }, where the color proportions in V satisfy

and c i (V ) denotes the number of vertices of color c i in V . A clustering T = {T 1 , . . . , T m } of V is called a p-divisible clustering if, for every cluster T i ∈ T and each color c j ∈ χ, the count c j (T i ) of vertices of color c j in T i is divisible by p j ; that is, p j | c j (T i ).

In the special case of two colors-blue and red-where the global ratio of blue to red vertices is p : 1, a p-divisible clustering T ensures that, for every cluster T i ∈ T , the number of blue vertices |blue (T i ) | is a multiple of p. We use the abbreviation pdc to denote a p-divisible clustering.
A clustering T is said to be δ-close pdc to an arbitrary unfair clustering D if
div.formula: dist(D, T ) ≤ δ • dist(D, T * ),
div.p: where T * denotes the closest pdc to D. Finally, we complement our upper bound result by showing that the problem becomes NP-hard when the ratio between the number of blue and red vertices is p : q with p ̸ = q.

div.head: Creating a p-divisible clustering.
div.p: In this section, given a clustering C = {C 1 , . . . , C m } of a set of red-blue colored vertices, where the irreducible ratio of blue to red vertices is p for some integer p > 1, we construct a pdc T = {T 1 , T 2 , . . . , T ζ }. Our main result for this section is the following: Lemma 3.1.1. There exists a polynomial time algorithm that, given any clustering C on n colored vertices with each vertex having a color either red or blue and a non-negative integer p, finds its 3.5-close pdc.
We provide the algorithm to find a 3.5-close pdc in Section 3.1.1 and provide the analysis of the algorithm in Section 3.1.2

div.head: Details of the Algorithm
div.p: Before describing our algorithm, let us first introduce a few notations that we use later.

For any input cluster C i , if its number of blue vertices is not a multiple of p, then we define its surplus as the minimum number of blue vertices whose removal makes the number of blue vertices a multiple of p, and we define its deficit as the minimum number of blue vertices whose addition makes the number of blue vertices to be a multiple of p. Formally, we define them as follows.
• Surplus of C i , s(C i ): For any cluster
div.formula: C i ⊆ V , s(C i ) = |blue (C i ) | mod p.
div.p: • Deficit of C i , d(C i ): For any cluster
div.formula: C i ⊆ V if p ∤ |blue (C i ) | then d(C i ) = p -s(C i ) otherwise d(C i ) = 0.
div.p: We call the operation of taking some vertices, S (say) from a cluster C i , that is C i = C i \ S as cut and the operation of merging some vertices M (say) to a cluster C i that is C i = C i ∪ M as merge. Let us define some more terms that we need to describe our algorithms.
• Cut cost, κ(C i ): For any cluster
div.formula: C i ∈ C, κ(C i ) = (s(C i ) • (|C i | -s(C i )).
div.p: • Merge cost, µ(C i ): For any cluster
div.formula: C i ∈ C, µ(C i ) = d(C i ) • |C i |.
div.p: Description of the algorithm AlgoforGeneral. Given a clustering, C, we partition the clusters C i ∈ C into two types based on the s(C i ) value of the cluster C i . If s(C i ) ≤ p/2 we call these clusters as cut clusters and if s(C i ) > p/2 we call these clusters as merge clusters. Thus
div.formula: • cut = {C i | s(C i ) ≤ p/2}.
div.p: • merge = {C i | s(C i ) > p/2}.

We first sort the clusters C i ∈ merge based on the value of (κ(C i ) -µ(C i )) in non-increasing order. Our algorithm AlgoforGeneral cuts a set of s(C i ) blue vertices from each cluster C i ∈ cut and merges them to clusters in merge sequentially starting from the beginning in the sorted list. In each cluster C j ∈ merge, we merge a set of d(C j ) blue vertices. Now, we have two cases: after a certain vertex of time, the remaining set of clusters in cut becomes empty, and we are only left with some clusters in merge; in this case, we call our subroutine AlgoforMerge. To remove any ambiguity, we refer to the remaining clusters in merge at this vertex as merge ′ , and the set of clusters created from cut after cutting the surplus vertices s(C i ) from each cluster C i ∈ cut be newcut.

Another case is when the remaining set of clusters in merge becomes empty, and we are only left with some clusters in cut. In this case, we call our subroutine AlgoforCut. Again, To remove any ambiguity, we refer to the remaining set of clusters in cut as cut ′ .

div.head: Description of the Subroutine AlgoforMerge.
div.p: The subroutine AlgoforMerge takes as input two sets of clusters: newcut and merge ′ . Here, newcut denotes the set of clusters that have already become p-divisible after the initial phase of AlgoforGeneral, and merge ′ denotes the remaining clusters from merge whose number of blue vertices is not yet a multiple of p.
We begin by computing the total deficit of the clusters in merge ′ , defined as
div.formula: W = C j ∈merge ′ d(C j ).
div.p: Intuitively, W represents the total number of blue vertices that must be added (through merging) across all clusters in merge ′ to make them p-divisible.
For every cluster C k ∈ newcut ∪ merge ′ , we partition the set of blue vertices blue (C k ) into
div.formula: |blue (C k ) | -s(C k ) p
div.p: subsets of size p, and one remaining subset of size s(C k ). We number the subset of size s(C k ) as the 0th subset, and label all other subsets of size p sequentially starting from 1. We denote the zth subset of cluster C k by W m,z . Each subset W m,z is associated with a cutting cost defined as follows:
div.formula: κ 0 (C k ) = s(C k ) • (|C k | -s(C k )),
div.p: (cost for cutting the 0th subset), (3.1)
div.formula: κ z (C k ) = p • (|C k | -(zp + s(C k ))
div.p: ), (cost for cutting the zth subset, z ≥ 1).

The subroutine AlgoforMerge is invoked in the situation where only clusters in merge remain non-p-divisible. Ideally, we would prefer to perform merge operations for all clusters in merge, since for these clusters we have s(C i ) > p/2, which implies µ(C i ) < κ(C i ). However, in order to make every cluster C i ∈ merge satisfy the divisibility condition p | |blue (C i ) |, we must also perform cut operations on some clusters to supply the required blue vertices. Therefore, we choose to cut from clusters C i that have the smallest difference (κ(C i ) -µ(C i )), ensuring that the incurred cutting cost is not disproportionately large relative to their merging benefit.

After the main algorithm AlgoforGeneral terminates, all clusters in newcut are already pdivisible. Nevertheless, it may still be more cost-effective to cut subsets of size p from some of these clusters in newcut than from certain clusters in merge ′ . This means that the algorithm may cut from the same cluster multiple times if it minimizes the total cost.

At each iteration of AlgoforMerge, among all clusters C ℓ ∈ newcut ∪ merge ′ , the algorithm selects a cluster C k with the minimum cost associated with its least uncut subset W m,vm , where v m denotes the smallest index corresponding to a subset of size p not yet cut from C k . The cost of the subset W m,vm is defined as:
div.formula: cost(W m,vm ) = κ vm (C k ), if v m ≥ 1, κ 0 (C k ) -µ(C k ), if v m = 0. (3.2)
div.p: If multiple clusters have the same minimum cost, the algorithm breaks ties arbitrarily. Let C k be the selected cluster. The algorithm then cuts the subset W m,vm from C k . If C k ∈ merge ′ , it is subsequently removed from merge ′ and the subset W m,vm is merged sequentially into the first available clusters in merge ′ , which are maintained in non-increasing order of (κ(C i ) -µ(C i )).

The process continues iteratively until the total deficit W becomes zero. We later prove that exactly W/p subsets need to be cut to eliminate the entire deficit, thereby ensuring that all clusters become p-divisible.

div.head: Description of the Subroutine AlgoforCut.
div.p: The subroutine AlgoforCut takes as input the set of clusters cut ′ , which represents the remaining clusters in cut after the main algorithm AlgoforGeneral terminates. For each cluster C i ∈ cut ′ , the algorithm removes s(C i ) blue vertices-corresponding to its surplus-and collects these vertices to form new auxiliary clusters, each of size p. This process is repeated sequentially until, in every cluster C i ∈ cut ′ , the number of blue vertices becomes a multiple of p. As a result, all clusters in the final output satisfy the p-divisibility property.
We provide the pseudocode of the algorithms AlgoforGeneral, AlgoforCut, AlgoforMerge in Algorithm 4, Algorithm 6 and Algorithm 5 respectively. Let the output of the algorithm AlgoforGeneral be T .

Runtime analysis of AlgoforGeneral. The expensive step in the AlgoforGeneral is that in the first step of the algorithm, we sort the clusters in merge which would take O (|merge| log(|merge|)) = O(n log n) time. The algorithm uses a vertex v ∈ V at most twice, once while cutting the vertex v from its parent cluster C i ∈ C (say) and another when merging the vertex v to some cluster C j ̸ = C i . Hence, the cutting and merging process of the algorithm can take at most O(n) time (recall, |V | = n).

In the subroutine AlgoforMerge, at each iteration, the algorithm needs to find the cluster that has the minimum cost attached to its least-numbered subset. The find-Min operation can be done in O(1) by implementing a priority queue with a Fibonacci heap. Hence, overall the time complexity
div.formula: of AlgoforGeneral is O(|merge| log(|merge|) + |V |) = O(n log n).

div.head: Approximation Guarantee for AlgoforGeneral
div.p: In this section, we prove that dist(C, T ) ≤ 3.5 dist(C, T * ) which is stated formally in Lemma 3.1.1
Our proof is divided into the following two cases:
• Merge case: When C i ∈cut s(C i ) ≤ C j ∈merge d(C j ); and
• Cut case: When C i ∈cut s(C i ) > C j ∈merge d(C j ).
In Section 3.1.2, we argue that in the merge case dist(C, T ) ≤ 3 dist(C, T * ).
Lemma 3.1.2. If C i ∈cut s(C i ) ≤ C j ∈merge d(C j ), the algorithm AlgoforGeneral produces a pdc T such that dist(C, T ) ≤ 3 dist(C, T * ).
In Section 3.1.2, we argue that in the cut case dist(C, T ) ≤ 3.5 dist(C, T * ).

Proof. Suppose for a partition X i,j , |T * r j \ X i,j | > s i,j . To prove this first we construct M from T * such that dist(C, M) < dist(C, T * ). This would contradict the fact that T * is the closest pdc and thus we will conclude
div.formula: |T * r j \ X i,j | ≤ s i,j . Construction of M from T * : M = T * \ {T * r j } ∪ {(X i,j \ S i,j ), (T * r j \ (X i,j \ S i,j ))}.
div.p: That is M we remove the set T * r j from T * and add two sets (X i,j \ S i,j ) and (T * r j \ (X i,j \ S i,j )) where S i,j ⊆ blue (X i,j ) such that |S i,j | = s i,j .
Note that,
div.formula: dist(C, M) = dist(C, T * ) + |X i,j \ S i,j ||S i,j | -|X i,j \ S i,j ||T * r j \ X i,j |

• Reason behind the term |X i,j \ S i,j ||S i,j | : The pairs (u, v) such that u ∈ (X i,j \ S i,j ) and v ∈ S i,j are not counted in dist(C, T * ) because u and v are present in the same clusters C i ∈ C and T * r j ∈ T * . In M, since, these pairs u and v belongs to different clusters (X i,j \ S i,j ) and (T * r j \ (X i,j \ S i,j )) respectively, hence, these pairs are counted in dist(C, M).

• Reason behind the term |X i,j \S i,j ||T * r j \X i,j | : The pairs (u, v) such that u ∈ (X i,j \S i,j ) and v ∈ T * r j \ X i,j are counted in dist(C, T * ) because such pairs u and v are present in the different clusters in C but in the same cluster T * r j ∈ T * . In M, since, these pairs u and v belongs to different clusters (X i,j \ S i,j ) and (T * r j \ (X i,j \ S i,j )) respectively, hence, these pairs are not counted in dist(C, M). Now,

div.head: Making a p-divisible clustering fair.
div.p: Given a p-divisible clustering T = {T 1 , T 2 , . . . , T ζ }, where the vertex set V is partitioned into two color groups, blue and red, with the ratio of blue to red vertices being p : 1, our goal is to compute a closest fair clustering F * to T . Recall that a clustering is said to be fair if, in every cluster, the number of blue vertices is exactly p times the number of red vertices. Our main result in this section is stated below.

Lemma 3.2.1. Let p > 1 be an integer, and let the vertex set V be partitioned into two color groups, blue and red, such that the ratio of blue to red vertices is p : 1. Then, there exists a lineartime algorithm that, given any p-divisible clustering T , computes a 3-close fair clustering F to C. More specifically, dist(T , F) ≤ 3 • dist(T , F * ),
where F * denotes a closest fair clustering to T .
In Section 3.2.1, we introduce the algorithm MakeClustersFair (Algorithm 7), which takes T as its input, and outputs a fair cluster F. We analyze in Section 3.2.2 that dist(T , F) ≤ 3dist(T , F * ).

div.head: Details of the Algorithm
div.p: The high-level idea of MakeClustersFair (Algorithm 7) is the following. The pdc T is partitioned into two sets. Each cluster T i is chosen to be in one of Runtime Analysis of MakeClustersFair. First note, each vertex is used at most twice during the execution of the algorithm MakeClustersFair -once when we cut the red vertex v ∈ V from the cluster in the set RedHeavy and again when we merge that red vertex v ∈ V to cluster that belongs to the set BlueHeavy. Hence, the total runtime of the algorithm MakeClustersFair would be O(|V |).

div.head: Concluding the Approximation Guarantee
div.p: In this section, we prove Theorem 4 by combining the results of Lemma 3.2.1 and Lemma 3.1.1 to establish the overall approximation guarantee. Specifically, we show that the clustering F obtained by first applying AlgoforGeneral to the input clustering C to obtain T , and then applying MakeClustersFair to T , yields a 17-close fair clustering with respect to C. Instead of directly proving Theorem 4, we first prove the following lemma, which immediately implies Theorem 4 by setting the parameters δ = 3.5 and α = 3.

Lemma 3.3.1. Consider any δ, α ≥ 1. Suppose there is a t 1 (n)-time algorithm Algorithm-A() that, given any clustering on n points, produces an δ-close pdc, and a t 2 (n)-time algorithm Algorithm-B() that, given any pdc on n points, produces a α-close fair clustering. Then there is an O(t 1 (n) + t 2 (n) + n)-time algorithm that, given any clustering on n points, produces an (δ + α + δα)-close fair clustering.

Proof. Consider the following simple algorithm: Given a clustering C as input, first run Algorithm-A() to generate a pdc T , and then run Algorithm-B() with T as input to generate a fair clustering F. Finally, output F.

It is straightforward to see that the running time of the above algorithm is O(t 1 (n) + t 2 (n) + n). We now claim that F is an (δ + α + δα)-close fair clustering of the input clustering C. Let F * be an (arbitrary) closest fair clustering of the input C, and T * be an (arbitrary) closest pdc of the input C. Since by the definition, any fair clustering is also a pdc, we get dist(C, T * ) ≤ dist(C, F * ).
(3.57) Now, by the guarantee provided by Algorithm-A(), we get and that concludes the proof.

div.head: Hardness of Closest Fair Clustering Problem
div.p: In this section, we prove that given a clustering C over a set of n red-blue colored vertices where the ratio between the total number of blue and red vertices is p for some integer p > 1, the problem of finding a Closest fair clustering F * is NP-hard. More specifically, we prove Theorem 5, which we restate below.

Theorem 5. The closest fair clustering problem is NP-hard when the vertex set V is divided into two disjoint groups, blue and red, and the number of blue vertices is p times the number of red vertices, for some integer p > 1.

div.head: Let us start by defining the corresponding decision version of the problem.
div.p: Definition 3.4.1 (closest p-fair). Consider a positive integer p. Given a clustering C over a set of red-blue colored vertices where the ratio between the total number of blue and red vertices is p, and a non-negative integer τ , decide between the following:
• YES: There exists a fair clustering (on input vertex set) F such that dist(C, F ) ≤ τ ;
• NO: For every fair clustering (on input vertex set) F , dist(C, F ) > τ .
We show the following theorem.
Lemma 3.4.2. For any integer p ≥ 2, the closest p-fair problem is NP-complete.
It is immediate from Lemma 3.4.2 that Theorem 5 follows as a direct consequence. Hence, we focus on establishing Lemma 3.4.2.

Observe that the closest p-fair problem clearly belongs to the class NP. To prove its NPhardness, we present a polynomial-time reduction from the well-known 3-Partition problem (defined below) to closest p-fair. This reduction establishes that closest p-fair is NP-complete.

Definition 3.4.3 (3-Partition problem). Given a (multi)set of positive integers S = {x 1 , . . . , x n }, decide whether (YES:) there exists a partition of S into m (disjoint) subsets S 1 , S 2 , . . . , S m ⊆ S where m = n/3, such that • For all i, |S i | = 3; and
• For all i, x j ∈S i x j = T , where T =
x j ∈S x j n/3 , or (NO:) no such partition exists.

Note that, by partition of S we mean S i ∩ S j = ∅ for all i ̸ = j and m i=1 S i = S. We know that the 3-Partition problem is in fact strongly NP-complete [GJ75], i.e., the 3-Partition problem remains NP-complete even if all the integers x i ∈ S are bounded by a polynomial in n; more specifically, max x i ∈S x i ≤ n c for some non-negative constant c. Furthermore, the 3-Partition problem remains strongly NP-complete even when for all x i ∈ S, x i ∈ (T /4, T /2), where T = 3 n x i ∈S x i [GJ75]. From now on, we refer to this restricted (with a restriction that each x i ∈ (T /4, T /2)) variant of the 3-partition problem as the 3partition problem.

div.head: Theorem 15. ([GJ75]) 3partition is strongly NP-complete.
div.p: We divide our NP-hardness proof into two parts. First, we prove closest p-fair is NP-hard for any integer p ≥ 3, and then we prove closest p-fair is NP-hard also for p = 2 using a slightly different reduction.

div.head: Hardness of closest p-fair for p ≥ 3:
div.p: In this section, we prove the following lemma.
Lemma 3.4.4. For any integer p ≥ 3, the closest p-fair problem is NP-hard.
To prove Lemma 3.4.4, we show a reduction from 3partition to closest p-fair.

Reduction from 3partition to closest p-fair : Let us consider a 3partition instance S = {x 1 , x 2 , . . . , x n }, where for all i ∈ [n], x i ≤ n c , for some non-negative constant c. Given the 3partition instance S = {x 1 , x 2 , . . . , x n } we create a closest p-fair instance (C, τ ) as follows:

• C = {B 1 , . . . , B n/3 , R 1 , . . . , R n }, where for each i ∈ {1, . . . , n/3}, B i is a monochromatic blue cluster (i.e., containing only blue vertices) of size pT and for each j ∈ {1, . . . , n}, R j is a monochromatic red cluster (i.e., containing only red vertices) of size x j (i.e.,
div.formula: |R j | = x j ); • τ = 1 2 n j=1 x j (T -x j ) + n 3 pT 2 .
div.p: Since each x i ≤ n c , the size of the instance (C, τ ) is polynomial in n. Moreover, it is straightforward to see that the reduction runs in polynomial time.
Now, we argue that the above reduction maps a YES instance of the 3partition to a YES instance of the closest p-fair.
Lemma 3.4.5. If S is a YES instance of the 3partition, then (C, τ ) is also a YES instance of the closest p-fair.
Proof. Suppose S is a YES instance of the 3partition.
Then there exists a partition S 1 , S 2 , . . . , S n/3 of S = {x 1 , x 2 , . . . , x n } such that for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n/3, |S i | = 3 and
div.formula: x j ∈S i x j = T where T = x k ∈S x k n 3 .
div.p: Let, S i = {x i 1 , x i 2 , x i 3 }. By our construction of (C, τ ), we have |R i j | = x i j , for j ∈ {1, 2, 3}. Now, we construct a fair clustering F by merging each B i with R i 1 , R i 2 , R i 3 . More formally,
Note that F is a fair clustering because for each cluster F ∈ F we have |blue (F ) | = pT (since blue (F ) = B i for some i ∈ [n/3]) and
Next, we claim that
div.formula: dist(C, F) = 1 2 n j=1 x j (T -x j ) + n 3 pT 2 = τ.
div.p: • Reason behind the term 1 2 n j=1 x j (T -x j ): In F , each red cluster R j is merged with (T -|R j |) red vertices from other clusters. This expression counts the number of such pairs. 1/2 comes from the fact that we are counting a pair twice, once while considering the cluster R j and again while considering a cluster R j ′ , for j ′ ̸ = j, that is merged with R j . (One important thing to note is that since S is a YES instance of the 3partition, we do not need to cut any red cluster R j in C to form the fair clustering F .)
• Reason behind the term (n/3)pT 2 : To form each cluster of F we have merged T red vertices with pT blue vertices. We have n/3 clusters in F, hence the number of such pairs in total is (n/3)pT 2 .
Hence, (C, τ ) is a YES instance of the closest p-fair.
Now, we argue that our reduction maps a NO instance of the 3partition to a NO instance of the closest p-fair.
Lemma 3.4.6. For p ≥ 3, if S is a NO instance of the 3partition, then (C, τ ) is also a NO instance of the closest p-fair.
Proof. To prove (C, τ ) is a NO instance of the closest p-fair we consider an (arbitrary) closest fair clustering F * to C, and then argue that dist(C, F * ) > τ .

Let us recall, S = {x 1 , . . . , x n }, C = {B 1 , . . . , B n/3 , R 1 , . . . , R n } where B i 's are monochromatic blue clusters each of size pT , where T = x i ∈S x i /(n/3) and for each ℓ ∈ [n], R ℓ is a monochromatic red cluster of size x ℓ .
To prove dist(C, F * ) > τ we prove the following claim regarding the structure of F * when p ≥ 3.
Claim 3.4.7. Consider any integer p ≥ 3. Then, for all B i , there exists F a ∈ F * such that blue (F a ) = B i .
For now, let us assume the above claim and prove Lemma 3.4.6. Since, the number of monochromatic blue clusters in C is n/3, assuming Claim 3.4.7 we get |F * | = n/3.

According to the definition of consensus metric, dist(C, F * ) counts total number of pairs (u, v) that are together in C but separated by F * and the number of pairs (u, v) that are in different clusters in C but together in F * .
For a cluster F a ∈ F * , let us define cost(F a ) to be the number of pairs u, v such that u, v ∈ F a but in different clusters in C.
Formally, we define cost(F a ) as
div.formula: cost(F a ) := |{(u, v) | u, v ∈ F a but u ∈ C i , v ∈ C j , C i , C j ∈ C, i ̸ = j}|.
div.p: It is easy to verify that

Proof of Lemma 3.4.4. By Lemma 3.4.5 and Lemma 3.4.6 we infer that for any p ≥ 3, S is a YES instance of the 3partition if and only if (C, τ ) is a YES instance of the closest p-fair. It now immediately follows from our reduction that for any p ≥ 3, closest p-fair is NP-hard because 3partition is strongly NP-complete (Theorem 15).

Remark 3.4.13. We would like to remark that the above NP-hardness proof can be extended for any fixed p/q ratio on the input blue to red vertices as long as p/q > 1 + √ 2. More specifically, consider any two integers p, q ≥ 2 such that p/q > 1 + √ 2. Then the closest fair clustering problem on red-blue colored vertices where the ratio between the total number of blue and red vertices is p/q, is NP-hard. We can show this result by making the following modifications to the reduction:

3.4.2 Hardness of closest p-fair for p = 2:
In this section, we prove the following lemma.
Lemma 3.4.14. For p = 2, the closest p-fair problem is NP-hard.

We again reduce the 3partition problem to the closest p-fair problem for the case when p = 2. The reduction follows the same structure as in the case where p ≥ 3, with the only difference being the choice of the parameter τ . For completeness, we restate the reduction here.

Reduction from 3partition to closest p-fair: Consider a 3partition instance S = {x 1 , x 2 , . . . , x n }, where for all i ∈ [n], it holds that x i ≤ n c for some fixed non-negative constant c. Given this instance, we construct a corresponding closest p-fair instance (C, τ ) as follows:
• Define the set of clusters as
where each B i (for i ∈ {1, . . . , n/3}) is a monochromatic blue cluster of size pT , and each R j (for j ∈ {1, . . . , n}) is a monochromatic red cluster of size x j , i.e., |R j | = x j .
• Set the value of τ as
div.formula: τ = p n ℓ=1 x 2 ℓ + p 2 2 n ℓ=1 x ℓ (T -x ℓ )
div.p: Since, for all i ∈ [n], it holds that x i ≤ n c for some fixed non-negative constant c, it is straightforward to see that the above reduction is a polynomial time reduction. Now, we argue that the above reduction maps a YES instance of the 3partition to a YES instance of the closest p-fair.
Lemma 3.4.15. If S is a YES instance of the 3partition, then (C, τ ) is also a YES instance of the closest p-fair.
Proof. Suppose S is a YES instance of the 3partition.

Claim 3.4.17. There exists ℓ, a 1 , a 2 such that x a 1 ,ℓ , x a 2 ,ℓ ̸ = 0.
Proof. For the sake of contradiction, suppose for all ℓ, there exists at most one F a ∈ F * such that x a,ℓ ̸ = 0.
Since Fa∈F * x a,ℓ = x ℓ , we have a cluster F a ∈ F * such that x a,ℓ = x ℓ . Now we create partitions S i of S in the following way: For each B i ∈ C,

• S a = S (since x a,ℓ cannot be zero for all a).
Since |B i | = pT and all clusters F a ∈ F * such that blue (F a ) ⊆ B i are fair we have,

div.p: Further, since each x ℓ ∈ (T /4, T /2), we must have |S i | = 3. However, since S is a NO instance of 3partition, such a partitioning of S does not exist, leading to a contradiction.
Hence, we conclude that there must exist ℓ, a 1 , a 2 such that x a 1 ,ℓ , x a 2 ,ℓ ̸ = 0.
Thus we finally get that dist(C, F * ) > τ , which implies (C, τ ) is a NO instance of the closest p-fair, for p = 2.
Similar to the proof of Lemma 3.4.4, we conclude the proof of Lemma 3.4.14.

Proof of Lemma 3.4.14. By Lemma 3.4.15 and Lemma 3.4.16 we infer that for any p = 2, S is a YES instance of the 3partition if and only if (C, τ ) is a YES instance of the closest p-fair. It now immediately follows from our reduction that for any p = 2, closest p-fair is NP-hard because 3partition is strongly NP-complete ( Theorem 15).

div.head: Chapter 4
div.p: Closest Fair Clustering with more than Two Colors

In this chapter, we find an approximate closest fair clustering to given clustering C, when the vertex set V is divided into multiple colored disjoint groups χ = {c 1 , . . . , c d }. We use the notation σ(v) to denote the color assigned to v from χ.

div.head: Approximate Closest Fair Clustering for Equi-Proportion Groups
div.p: In this section, we provide an approximation algorithm to find a closest fair clustering when all the groups are of equal size. More specifically we prove Theorem 6, which we restate below.

Theorem 6. Let χ be a set of colors and let V be partitioned into disjoint color classes indexed by χ, such that each color class has the same size and |χ| > 2, then there exists a polynomialtime algorithm that computes an O(|χ| 1.6 log 2.81 |χ|)-close fair clustering with respect to a given input clustering C. Moreover, when |χ| is a power of two, the algorithm computes a O(|χ| 1.6 )-close fair clustering.

First, let us handle the case when |χ| is a power of 2. To do that, we provide an algorithm fairpower-of-two, which produces an O(|χ| 1.6 )-close fair clustering F fpt to a clustering C when |χ| is a power of 2.

div.head: Details of the Algorithm: Power-of-Two Colors
div.p: Let the input of the algorithm fairpower-of-two be a clustering C = {C 1 , C 2 , . . . , C m }, where each cluster C a ∈ C consists of points colored from a color set χ = {c 1 , c 2 , . . . , c d }. We assume that the number of colors |χ| is a power of two.

The goal is to produce a fair clustering F fpt such that, in each cluster F a ∈ F fpt , the number of points of each color is equal, that is c p (F a ) = c q (F a ) where p ̸ = q and c r (F a ) denotes the number of points of color c r in F a .
The algorithm proceeds in log |χ| iterations, indexed by i = 1 to log |χ|. In each iteration, the color set χ = {c 1 , . . . , c |χ| } is partitioned into blocks of size 2 i :

(Note: This defines |χ|/2 i blocks in total.) Let, after iteration i of the algorithm fairpower-of-two the input clustering C is changed to a clustering N i . The algorithm fairpower-of-two at each iteration i maintains an invariant that for every block B i j and for every cluster N i a ∈ N i , the number of points of each color within B i j is equal in N i a . Formally, for all x, y ∈ {1, . . . , 2 i } with x ̸ = y, we have:
div.formula: c (j-1)•2 i +x (N i a ) = c (j-1)•2 i +y (N i a ),
div.p: where c r (N i a ) denotes the number of points of color c r in cluster N i a . Hence, after log |χ| iterations when there is only one block, we have that for the clustering N log |χ| = F fpt in each cluster F a ∈ F fpt , the number of points of each color is equal.
Let us now describe the algorithm fairpower-of-two which maintains the above invariant. To describe the algorithm first we need to define some notations.
• As described previously the clustering C changes at each iteration i of the algorithm fairpower-of-two.
Let, N i = {N i 1 , N i 2 , . . . , N i z } be the clustering formed at iteration i. Specifically, the clustering C goes through the following transformations.
div.formula: C → N 1 → N 2 → • • • → N log |χ| = F fpt .

div.formula: B i j (N i a ) = {v ∈ N i a | σ(v) ∈ B i j }

div.head: Now we are ready to describe the algorithm fairpower-of-two
div.p: Description of fairpower-of-two: The algorithm proceeds in log |χ| iterative phases to enforce fairness across pairs of buckets. The high-level structure of the algorithm is as follows:
1. Initialization: Set the initial clustering N 0 = {N 0 1 , N 0 2 , . . . , N 0 f } = C (input of fairpower-of-two).
2. Iterative Refinement: For each phase i = 1 to log |χ|: (a) Initialize N i as a copy of N i-1 .
(b) Iterate over j = 1 to |χ|/2 i in steps of 2 i : i. For each cluster N i a ∈ N i :
• Compute the surplus between the bucketed subsets B i j (N i a ) and B i j+1 (N i a ) i , defined as T j a .
• Remove this surplus from N i a .
• Store the removed surplus in set
div.formula: S j if |B i j (N i a )| ≥ |B j+1 (N i a ) i |, else store it in S j+1 .
div.p: ii. Merge the stored surpluses using the subroutine multi-GM(S j , S j+1 ) to form new fair clusters. iii. Add the resulting clusters of the multi-GM step back to N i .

div.head: Output: Return the final fair clustering N log |χ| .
div.p: Remarks. The algorithm ensures local fairness between adjacent buckets B i j and B i j+1 by removing and redistributing surplus elements. As the phases progress, the granularity of this balancing increases, resulting in a globally fair clustering. The multi-GM subroutine plays a key role in recombining the surplus elements in a way that preserves fairness across buckets.
Let us now describe the multi-gm algorithm.
Cescription of multi-gm: multi-gm is a procedure that takes as input two collections of point sets:
• Set1: a set of point subsets whose elements have colors from a color block B i j ,
• Set2: a set of point subsets whose elements have colors from the adjacent color block B i j+1 .

Each block B i j and B i j+1 contains the same number of colors. The goal is to iteratively pair subsets from Set1 and Set2 to form new subsets that are locally fair, meaning each resulting subset has an equal number of points from each color in the union of B i j ∪ B i j+1 . These fair subsets are returned as a new collection.
The algorithm proceeds greedily by:
• Iteratively selecting one subset from each of Set1 and Set2.
• Comparing their sizes and extracting a balanced subset from the larger set to match the size of the smaller one.
• Merging the two into a fair subset and adding it to the output collection.
• Updating or removing the subsets used and repeating this process until no more valid pairings are possible.

The final output is a collection of fair subsets, each containing an equal number of points of every color from B i j ∪ B i j+1 . We provide the pseudocode of the algorithms fairpower-of-two and multi-gm in Algorithm 8 and Algorithm 9 respectively.

• If x > y, merge p b k • (x -y) points of color z b k into F t-1 for each k ∈ [u].

This ensures that the scaling factor for both sub-blocks becomes equal (x in both the cases), aligning the entire block B t i to the correct global ratio structure. We provide the pseudocode of make-pdc-fair in Algorithm 10.

Let us now describe the algorithm fair-equi. The algorithm fair-equi takes a clustering C as input. Each vertex of the clustering is colored from the colors χ = {c 1 , c 2 , . . . , c d } where |χ| is not a power of two.

Description of the algorithm fair-equi: We divide χ into log |χ| many disjoint color groups G 1 , G 2 , . . . , G log |χ| such that the size of each group, |G j | where j ∈ [log |χ|] is a power of two. We do it greedily according to the binary representation of |χ|. Consider the binary representation of |χ|. For each index j ∈ [log⌈|χ|⌉], if the corresponding bit is 1, create a group of size 2 j-1 .

We apply the algorithm fairpower-of-two to get an intermediate clustering I = {I 1 , . . . , I η } such that for each cluster I j ∈ I where j ∈ For a subset S ⊆ V , let us define G ℓ (S) as the set of vertices v ∈ S such that v has a color in G ℓ . Now, our goal is to get a clustering F = {F 1 , . . . , F ι } from C such that for each cluster F k ∈ F we have c u (F k ) = c v (F k ) where c u , c v ∈ χ.
Given the intermediate clustering I as input, the algorithm make-pdc-fair produces a final fair clustering F = {F 1 , . . . , F ι } and thus for each cluster F j ∈ F, the following proportion holds.

To apply make-pdc-fair, we consider a group of colors G ℓ as a single metacolor z ℓ . Here the clustering I is a p-divisible clustering because for any cluster I j ∈ I we have |G ℓ (I j )| is divisible by
div.formula: |G ℓ |.
div.p: Furthermore, the algorithm make-pdc-fair ensures uniformity within each group: for every group G ℓ and for any pair of colors c a , c b ∈ G ℓ with ℓ ∈ [log |χ|], it guarantees that c a (F j ) = c b (F j ). As a consequence, for any pair of colors c u , c v ∈ χ, we have c u (F j ) = c v (F j ), i.e., each color is equally represented within every cluster of F.
