Proof of Theorem 6. To prove this theorem, we analyse the algorithm fair-equi. The algorithm fair-equi takes a clustering C as input, applies the algorithm fairpower-of-two as a subroutine to create an intermediate clustering I and then applies the subroutine make-pdc-fair to get the final fair clustering F.

By Lemma 4.1.7 we get that, F is O(log 2.8 |χ|)-close to the clustering I. By Lemma 4.1.1 we get that I is O(|χ| 1.6 )-close to the clustering C. By applying the triangle inequality to the two preceding results, we conclude that the output clustering F produced by fair-equi is O(|χ| 1.6 log 2.8 |χ|)-close to the input clustering C.
Let F * be the closest fair clustering to C. Hence, we get, dist(C, F) ≤ dist(C, I) + dist(I, F ) (triangle inequality) ≤ dist(C, I) + O(log

2.8 |χ|)dist(I, F * ) ≤ O(|χ| 1.6 )dist(C, F * ) + O(log 2.8 |χ|)dist(I, F * ) ≤ O(|χ| 1.6 )dist(C, F * ) + O(log 2.8 |χ|)(dist(C, I) + dist(C, F * )) (triangle inequality) ≤ O(|χ| 1.6 log 2.8 |χ| + |χ| + log 2.8 |χ|)dist(C, F * ) ≤ O(|χ| 1.6 log 2.8 |χ|)dist(C, F * ) This completes the proof of Theorem 6.

div.head: Approximate Closest Fair Clustering for Arbitrary-Proportion Groups
div.p: In this section, we extend our analysis from the equiproportion setting to the general case where color groups may appear in arbitrary proportions. In this setting, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm to compute an approximate closest fair clustering to a given input clustering C. More specifically, we prove Theorem 7, which we restate below.

Theorem 7. There is a polynomial time algorithm that, given an arbitrary clustering C over a vertex set V where each vertex v ∈ V has a color in χ = {c 1 , . . . , c k }, finds an O(|χ| 3.81 )-close fair clustering to the clustering C.
To prove the above theorem, we take a 2-step approach similar to Chapter 3, which was constrained to only two colors.
(i) First, we convert the clustering C to a clustering M such that for each cluster M i ∈ M, c j (M i ) is divisible by p j . Recall, we call such a clustering a p-divisible clustering.
(ii) In the second step, we will provide the clustering M as input to the algorithm make-pdc-fair and get a fair clustering F as output.

Now, let us describe the fair-general that computes an approximate closest fair clustering to a given input clustering C. We first describe a subroutine create-pdc that converts a clustering C on a vertex set V to a p-divisible clustering M.

div.head: Details of the Algorithm
div.p: To describe the algorithm create-pdc, let us define some terms.

• σ(C k , c j ): Surplus of C k w.r.t. to the color c j , formally, σ(C k , c j ) ⊆ C k that contains c j (C k ) mod p j points of color c j if p j ∤ c j (C k ), otherwise it contains p j points of color c j .
• σ j = C k ∈C σ(C k , c j ) (Note σ j must be a multiple of p j )
• δ(C k , c j ): Ceficit of C k w.r.t. to the color c j , δ(C k , c j ) ⊆ V \ C k that contains p j -|σ(C k , c j )| points.
• κ j (C k ): Cut cost of C k w.r.t. a color c j , formally
div.formula: κ j (C k ) = |σ(C k , c j )|(|C k | -|σ(C k , c j )|) • µ j (C k ): Merge cost of C k w.r.t. a color c j , formally µ j (C k ) = |δ(C k , c j )|(|C k |)
div.p: Now, let's discuss the algorithm create-pdc. Input: A clustering C of data points, a set of colors χ = {c 1 , c 2 , . . . , c d }, and a desired proportion vector p = (p 1 , . .
div.formula: . , p d ) such that c 1 (V ) : c 2 (V ) : • • • : c d (V ) = p 1 : p 2 : • • • : p d .
div.p: Goal: Convert the input clustering C into a p-divisible clustering M where each cluster contains a multiple of p j points for each color c j .
Description of the subroutine create-pdc:
• For each color c j , prepare σ j /p j empty extra clusters {P 1 , P 2 , . . . , P σ j /p j }

First, we apply the algorithm create-pdc to the input clustering C to obtain a p-divisible clustering M that is O(|χ|)-close to C (by Lemma 4.2.1). Then, we apply the algorithm make-pdc-fair on M to obtain the final fair clustering F, which is O(|χ| 2.81 )-close to M (by Lemma 4.1.7). div.head: Implications to Weighted Fair Correlation and Fair Consensus Clustering
div.p: Building on the algorithms developed in the previous sections that compute an α-close fair clustering for a given (possibly unfair) clustering D, we now show how these results can be leveraged to obtain approximation algorithms for the weighted fair correlation clustering and fair consensus clustering problems.

div.head: Implication to weighted Fair Correlation Clustering
div.p: In this section, we present an algorithm for computing an approximate weighted fair correlation clustering, assuming access to a procedure that can compute an α-close fair clustering for any given (potentially unfair) clustering D. We further provide a detailed analysis of the algorithm and establish its approximation guarantee. Specifically, we prove the following result.

Theorem 2. Suppose we have an algorithm to find an α-close fair clustering to any given unfair clustering D, then given a correlation clustering instance G , there exists an algorithm to find an (α + ρ + αρ) -approximate weighted fair correlation clustering under probability constraints, where ρ is the state-of-the-art approximation factor for the weighted correlation clustering problem under probability constraints.
Proof. Let us first describe the algorithm fairfyCC, which computes a fair clustering for a given weighted correlation clustering instance G.
• Input: Weighted Correlation clustering instance G.
• Output: A fair clustering F.
• Procedure:
1. Compute a clustering D from the weighted insatnce G using a ρ-approximation algorithm to find an unfair correlation clustering on a weighted instance.
2. Apply the closest fair clustering algorithm to D to obtain a fair clustering F that is α-close to D. 3. Return F .
Let us now prove that F is (α + ρ + αρ) approximate fair correlation clustering of G. We know for a weighted correlation clustering instance G, by definition for a clustering K on G we have
div.formula: cost(K) = u∼ K v w -(u, v) + u≁ K v w + (u, v)
div.p: recall where u ∼ K v denotes that u and v are together in the clustering K and u ≁ K v denotes that they are separated in K.
Let F * corr be the optimal fair correlation clustering of G. We need to prove that cost(F) ≤ (α + ρ + αρ) cost(F * corr ).
To show the above, we need to prove the following claims Claim 5.1.1. For any two arbitrary clusterings M and K on a vertex set V we have cost(M) ≤ dist(M, K) + cost(K)
Proof. We have
div.formula: cost(M) = u∼ M v w -(u, v) + u≁ M v w + (u, v) = u∼ M v ∧u∼ K v w -(u, v) + u∼ M v ∧u≁ K v w -(u, v) + u≁ M v ∧u∼ K v w + (u, v) + u≁ M v ∧u≁ K v w + (u, v)
div.p: Again, similarly, we have,
div.formula: cost(K) = u∼ K v ∧u∼ M v w -(u, v) + u∼ K v ∧u≁ M v w -(u, v) + u≁ K v ∧u∼ M v w + (u, v) + u≁ K v ∧u≁ M v w + (u, v)
div.p: We also have,
div.formula: dist(M, K) = u∼ M v ∧u≁ K v 1 + u≁ M v ∧u∼ K v 1 Hence, cost(K) + dist(M, K) = u∼ M v ∧u≁ K v (1 + w + (u, v)) + u≁ M v ∧u∼ K v (1 + w -(u, v)) + u∼ K v ∧u∼ M v w -(u, v) + u≁ K v ∧u≁ M v w + (u, v)
div.p: ≥ cost(M) (since w + (u, v), w -(u, v) ≤ 1) Claim 5.1.2. For any two arbitrary clusterings M and K on a vertex set V we have dist(M, K) ≤ cost(M) + cost(K)
Proof. We have
div.formula: dist(M, K) = u∼ M v ∧u≁ K v 1 + u≁ M v ∧u∼ K v 1 cost(M) = u∼ M v ∧u∼ K v w -(u, v) + u∼ M v ∧u≁ K v w -(u, v) + u≁ M v ∧u∼ K v w + (u, v) + u≁ M v ∧u≁ K v w + (u, v)and

cost(K) = u∼ K v ∧u∼ M v w -(u, v) + u∼ K v ∧u≁ M v w -(u, v) + u≁ K v ∧u∼ M v w + (u, v) + u≁ K v ∧u≁ M v w + (u, v) Hence, cost(M) + cost(K) = u∼ K v ∧u∼ M v 2w -(u, v) + u∼ K v ∧u≁ M v 1 + u≁ K v ∧u∼ M v 1 + u≁ K v ∧u≁ M v 2w + (u, v) (since, w + (u, v) + w -(u, v) = 1)
div.p: ≥ dist(M, K)
Now we are ready to prove Theorem 2.

• The inequality Eq. (5.1) is by Claim 5.1.1.
• The inequality Eq. (5.2) is since D is ρ-approximate correlation clustering.
• The inequality Eq. (5.3) is since F is α-approximate closest fair to D.

• The inequality Eq. (5.5) is by Claim 5.1.2.

div.head: Implication to Fair Consensus Clustering
div.p: In this section, we present an algorithm for computing an approximate fair consensus clustering, assuming access to a procedure that can compute an α-close fair clustering for any given (potentially unfair) clustering D. We also provide a detailed analysis of the algorithm and establish its approximation guarantee. Specifically, we prove the following result.

Theorem 3. Suppose we have an algorithm to find an α-close fair clustering to any given unfair clustering D, then given m input clusterings, C 1 , . . . , C m , there exists an algorithm to find an (α + 2)-approximate fair consensus clustering.

Proof. Let us consider the following algorithm: Suppose we are given m clusterings C 1 , . . . , C m . Then, for each C i , compute an α-close fair clustering F i . Then, output the fair clustering F k that minimizes the ℓ-mean objective function, i.e.,
div.formula: F k = arg min i   m j=1 (dist(C j , F i )) ℓ   1/ℓ .
div.p: It remains to argue that the above algorithm achieves (α+2)-approximation to the fair consensus clustering problem.

Let F * con be an (arbitrary) optimal fair consensus clustering, and let C i * be a closest (breaking ties arbitrarily) clustering among C 1 , C 2 , • • • , C m , to F * con . We emphasize that we consider C i * only for the sake of the analysis. Since F * con is a fair clustering, we get dist(C i * , F i * ) ≤ α • dist(C i * , F * con ).
We next derive the following (dist(C j , F * con ) + dist(C j , F * con ) + α • dist(C j ,
div.formula: F * con )) ℓ   1/ℓ (Since C i * is closest to F * con ) = (α + 2)   m j=1 (dist(C j , F * con )) ℓ   1/ℓ .
div.p: Now, since our algorithm outputs F k that minimizes the ℓ-mean objective function, the approximation guarantee follows, and that concludes the proof.

div.head: Fair Consensus Clustering in Streaming setting
div.p: In this chapter, we present an algorithm algo-fair-con-stream for solving fair consensus clustering in a streaming setting. Recall in the fair consensus clustering problem, the input is the set of clusterings I = {C 1 , . . . , C m } on a set of vertices V (with |V | = n) and our goal is to output a fair clustering F , such that
div.formula: m i=1 dist(C i , F) ℓ 1/ℓ ≤ β m i=1 dist(C i , F * con ) ℓ 1/ℓ
div.p: where F * con is an optimal fair consensus clustering, the distance, dist(•, •) between two clusterings is the measured by the number of pairs (u, v) that are together in one clustering but separated by the other, and β ∈ R >1 , ℓ ∈ Z >1 are some parameters.
Let us now describe the streaming model. We consider an insertion-only streaming model. The input is a sequence of triples (p, j, b), where:
• p = (u, v) is an unordered pair of vertices in V ,
• j ∈ [m] identifies a clustering C j ∈ I, and • b ∈ {0, 1} indicates whether u and v lie in the same cluster in the clustering C j (b = 0) or in different clusters (b = 1).

Here, a triple ((u, v), j, b) refers an information about the clustering C j . For each clustering C j , we have n 2 such tuples, hence the length of the stream is mn 2 . These triples (p, j, b) can arrive in any arbitrary order. Let us name the above streaming model as pairwise streaming model. Our main result is stated in the following theorem.

Theorem 11. Suppose there exists an approximation algorithm for fair correlation clustering with running time t 1 (n), and assume oracle access to an α-approximate closest fair clustering algorithm. Then, there exists a (α + 1.995)-approximation algorithm for fair consensus clustering in the pairwise streaming model that uses O(n log m) space and has query time O n 2 log 4 m + t 1 (n) log 3 m .

div.head: Details of the algorithm: algo-fair-con-stream
div.p: In this section, we present our streaming algorithm, algo-fair-con-stream for fair consensus clustering. The algorithm relies on a subroutine, denoted by find-candidates, which we describe first.

The subroutine find-candidates takes as input a set of clusterings I and outputs a set of candidate clusterings F. The crucial guarantee is that F contains at least one fair clustering F that achieves a good approximation. The subroutine find-candidates assumes access to an α-close fair clustering algorithm.

The candidate set F is constructed as follows. For each clustering C i ∈ I, we include its α-close fair clustering F C i in F. In addition, for every ordered triple T = {C i , C j , C k } ∈ I × I × I, we add to F a clustering T i,j,k obtained by applying the subroutine ClusterFitting to T .
The pseudocodes of find-candidates and ClusterFitting are given in Algorithm 2 and Algorithm 3, respectively.
5 return T i,j,k Now we are ready to describe the algorithm algo-fair-con-stream. We work in the insertiononly stream described previously. The algorithm maintains two memory structures in parallel:

1. Sampled Store 1 (M 1 ): Prior to the arrival of the stream, we independently sample 4g log m indices j 1 , . . . , j 4g log m from [m] for some parameter g we fix the value of it later. For these sampled indices, all their corresponding triples that appear in the stream are stored in M 1 .

2. Sampled Store 2 (M 2 ): Similarly, before the stream starts, we sample 64ε -2 log m indices k 1 , . . . , k t from [m], where t = 64ε -2 log m and 0 < ε ≤ 1. For these sampled indices, all their triples are stored in M 2 as they appear in the stream.
After the stream ends.

1. We use union-find, to construct the clusterings C j 1 , . . . , C j log m from its triples stored in M 1 . Then we apply a subroutine find-candidates (Algorithm 2) on these ⌈log m⌉ clusterings to get a candidate set of fair clusterings F. The subroutine find-candidates assumes access to a α-close fair clustering algorithm.
2. We use union-find, to construct the clusterings C k 1 , . . . , C kt from its triples stored in M 2 . Let, W = {C k 1 , . . . , C kt }.
We use W to find the best fair clustering F ∈ F with respect to W, more specifically we find
div.formula: F = arg min F ′ ∈ F C i ∈W dist(C i , F ′ ) 3. Return F .
div.p: We provide the pseudocode of algo-fair-con-stream in the appendix.

div.head: Analysis of algo-fair-con-stream
div.p: In this section, we analyze the approximation guarantee of the algorithm algo-fair-con-stream, along with its time and space complexities.

div.head: Approximation Guarantee
div.p: We now establish the approximation guarantee of algo-fair-con-stream and thus prove Theorem 11. The Theorem 11 is obtained by appropriately instantiating the parameters in the following more general lemma.

Lemma 6.2.1. Suppose there exists an algorithm with running time t 2 (n) that, given a clustering over n points, computes an α-close fair clustering. Further, assume there exists an γ-approximation algorithm for fair correlation clustering on a graph with n vertices, running in time t 1 (n). Let η > 0, 0 < β < 1, c > 1, s > 1, and g > s be fixed parameters satisfying sc -s -2c > 0. Then, for any collection of m clusterings over n points, there exists a randomized algorithm that, with probability at least 1 -1 m , runs in time O n 2 log 4 m + t 1 (n) log 3 m , uses O(n log m) space, and outputs a 1+ε 1-ε • r -approximate fair consensus clustering, where r = max α + 2 -(α + 1)β, α + 2 + (α + 1) β(g -s) + s g(s -1) -2η c , α + 2 + (α + 1) β(g(2c + s) -sc) + sc g(cs -s -2c) -2 1 -1 s -1 c η, 1 + 3(γ + 1)η .

For each clustering C i , let I i denote the set of unordered vertex pairs (u, v) ∈ V × V such that u and v are clustered together (respectively, separated) in F * con , but are separated (respectively, clustered together) in C i . By definition, this implies

On the other hand, if (a, b) ∈ B, then a, b are separated (resp. together) if (a, b) is an edge in E + (G) (resp. E -(G)). Therefore, if for every pair (a, b) ∈ B, we flip their labels (from "+" to "-" and vice versa) we obtained a new graph G ′ such that, any two vertices in a same cluster in F * con are connected by an "+" edge, and any two vertices is different clusters in F * con are connected by a "-" edge. Note that, the correlation cost of a clustering C of G can be viewed as the number of pairs (a, b) whose labels need to be flipped so that, the edges inside every cluster of C are all "+" edges, and the edges between the clusters of C are all "-" edges. Hence, F * con has a correlation cost cost(F * con ) = |B|. Let T i,j,k be the output of ClusterFitting(T ) (Algorithm 3). In other words, T i,j,k is a clustering obtained by running a γ-approximation fair correlation clustering algorithm on G. Then cost(T i,j,k ) ≤ γ |B|, as the cost of an optimal fair correlation clustering is at most |B|. As a result, we get dist(T i,j,k , F * con ) ≤ |B| + γ |B| ≤ (1 + γ)3ηAVG (as |B| ≤ 3ηAVG).

div.head: Time and Space Complexity
div.p: Now we analyse the time and space complexity of the algorithm algo-fair-con-stream. Time Complexity. In M 1 we store log m many clusterings. Hence, there are O(log 3 m) many candidate clusterings in F. Computing a α-close fair clustering to each sampled clustering takes t 2 (n) log m time and running the procedure ClusterFitting on log 3 m triples of clusterings takes t 1 (n) log 3 m time. To find the best clustering in F, we need to perform O(log 3 m) many checks. Now, in each check, we need to compute the distance between two clusterings, which takes O(n 2 ) time, and since there are O(log m) clusterings in the W, the total time needed per check is O(n 2 log m). Hence, overall for all checks, the time needed is O(n 2 log 4 m). Hence, the overall time complexity is
div.formula: O(n 2 log 4 m + t 2 (n) log m + t 1 (n) log 3 m) = O(n 2 log 4 m + t 1 (n) log 3 m) (since t 1 (n) ≥ t 2 (n))
div.p: Space Complexity. In M 1 , we store information of ⌈log m⌉ many clusterings, hence we require a space of O(n log m) in M 1 . In M 2 also, we store O(log m) clusterings; hence, in M 2 , too we need O(n log m) space. Hence, overall, the space complexity is O(n log m).

div.head: Proof of Main Theorem
div.p: Now, we are ready to prove Theorem 11. To prove Theorem 11 we need to use Theorem 2. Recall Theorem 2 states that if there exists an algorithm to find α-close fair clustering to any given unfair clustering D, then given a correlation clustering instance G, there exists an algorithm to find an (α + ρ + αρ) -approximate fair correlation clustering, where ρ is the state-of-the-art approximation factor for the correlation clustering problem.

div.head: Open Problems
div.p: In this chapter, we highlight three compelling open directions that naturally arise from our study of closest fair clustering. These questions aim to deepen our understanding of fairness in clustering under different structural and algorithmic constraints.

div.head: Improving the Approximation Factor for Multiple Colors
div.p: In Theorem 6 and Theorem 7, we established algorithms for finding an α-close fair clustering where the approximation factor α depends polynomially on the number of color groups |χ|. While these results provide the first non-trivial guarantees for the multi-color setting, the dependence on |χ| can be undesirable-particularly when |χ| is large or comparable to the number of vertices |V |.

An intriguing open direction is to design algorithms whose approximation factor is independent of |χ|, that is, to obtain a constant-factor approximation for the closest fair clustering problem. Achieving such a result would represent a significant conceptual and technical advancement, as it would eliminate the combinatorial dependence on the number of protected groups.

Furthermore, as discussed in Chapter 5, a constant-factor approximation for the closest fair clustering problem would immediately imply constant-factor approximations for the fair correlation clustering and fair consensus clustering problems. This connection underscores the broader impact of improving the approximation factor in this setting. Question 7.1. Given a clustering C on a vertex set V , where V is partitioned into disjoint color groups χ = {c 1 , . . . , c d }, can we design an algorithm that computes an O(1)-close fair clustering F to C, independent of the number of colors d?

div.head: Extending to Alternative Fairness Notions
div.p: Several alternative definitions of fairness have been explored in the clustering literature, each motivated by different application scenarios and ethical considerations. One notable example is due to Ahmadian, Epasto, Kumar and Mahdian [AEK + 20], where each color c i is associated with a parameter σ i ∈ (0, 1). In their formulation, a clustering F is said to be fair if for every cluster F ∈ F we have c i (F ) ≤ σ i |F | for all i, recall c i (F ) denotes the number of vertices of color c i in F . This definition allows for flexible upper bounds on group representation rather than enforcing strict proportionality, thereby offering a more permissive and context-sensitive notion of fairness.

We refer to such definitions collectively as relaxed notions of fairness. For a given clustering C, we define F * C to be the closest relaxed fair clustering if dist(C, F * C ) ≤ dist(C, F ) for all clusterings F that satisfy any relaxed fairness criterion. While our results in previous sections address proportional fairness, it remains an intriguing question whether similar approximation guarantees can be achieved for these relaxed notions. This leads to the following open problem. Question 7.2. Given a clustering C on a vertex set V partitioned into disjoint color groups χ = {c 1 , . . . , c d }, can we design an approximation algorithm to compute the closest relaxed fair clustering F to C?

div.head: Handling Overlapping Subgroups
div.p: Fairness considerations in clustering often assume that the underlying demographic or protected groups form a disjoint partition of the dataset. However, in many real-world scenarios, individuals may belong to multiple groups simultaneously (for example, defined by intersections of gender, race, and age). This motivates the study of overlapping subgroup fairness, where the protected groups χ = {c 1 , . . . , c d } are not disjoint.

Ahmadian and Negahbani [AN23] studied this setting in the context of the fair correlation clustering problem. Their fairness definition is same as Ahmadian, Epasto, Kumar, and Mahdian [AEK + 20], where each color c i is associated with a parameter σ i ∈ (0, 1), and a clustering F is said to be fair if for every cluster F ∈ F we have c i (F ) ≤ σ i |F | for all i.

Ahmadian and Negahbani provided a bicriteria constant-factor approximation for the fair correlation clustering problem under this definition. Here, "bicriteria" means that fairness constraints are allowed to be slightly violated in some clusters, i.e.,
div.formula: c i (F ) ≤ (1 + ε) σ i |F |
div.p: for some small ε ∈ (0, 1).

A natural open question is whether similar bicriteria or exact guarantees can be achieved for the closest fair clustering problem under overlapping subgroup fairness. This would imply approximation for the fair consensus clustering problem. Question 7.3. Given a clustering C on a vertex set V , where the color groups χ = {c 1 , . . . , c d } may overlap (i.e., each vertex may belong to multiple protected groups), can we develop an approximation algorithm to find the closest relaxed fair clustering F to C? 8.5 Pseudocode of the algorithm fairpower-of-two Algorithm 8: fairpower-of-two(C) Input: Clustering C Output: A fair clustering F fpt 1 Let, N 0 = {N 0 1 , N 0 2 , . . . , N 0 ℓ } = C.

[CKL + 17] introduced the notion of fair clustering, requiring that the representation of sensitive groups within each cluster reflect their overall proportions in the dataset. Subsequent work expanded this framework: Bera et al. [BCF + 19] and Huang et al. [HJV19] developed improved algorithms for fair clustering, while Backurs et al. [BIV + 19] studied scalable approaches, Chen et al. [CFL + 19] introduced proportionally fair clustering, and Ahmadian et al. [AEK + 20] addressed correlation clustering under fairness constraints.

The study of fair clustering was initiated by Chierichetti et al. [CKL + 17], who introduced the fairlet framework for k-center/k-median/k-means clustering with two colors, later extended to multiple colors by Rösner and Schmidt [RS18]. Their proportional-fairness model requires that the demographic distribution within each cluster reflect the global proportions of the dataset. Building on this foundation, Ahmadian et al. [AEK + 20] proposed an alternative model where, for each color c i , the number of c i vertices in any cluster is bounded by a parameter σ i |F |, offering finer control of demographic representation. A number of subsequent works explored complementary formulations of fairness. Huang et al. [HJV19] introduced coreset constructions that preserve both cost and fairness constraints, enabling scalable fair k-median/k-means clustering. Backurs et al. [BIV + 19] developed scalable approximation algorithms that extend fairlet ideas to near-linear running time. Chen et al. [CFL + 19] studied proportionally fair clustering, requiring each cluster to approximately reflect global proportions, and provided bicriteria approximations. Bera et al. [BCF + 19] handled overlapping sensitive groups, ensuring fairness constraints are satisfied simultaneously for multiple (possibly intersecting) populations. Esmaeili et al. [EBT + 20] proposed a group-oblivious probabilistic model, relaxing hard constraints to fairness-in-expectation, useful when group memberships are uncertain. Beyond geometric clustering, fairness has also been studied in unweighted correlation clustering. Ahmadian et al. [AEK + 20] initiated this direction by incorporating fairness into the minimizedisagreements objective, followed by alternative formulations [AGS + 20] and improved guarantees [AN23]. Finally, fairness has been extended to rank aggregation, which can be viewed as 1-clustering over permutations. Wei et al. [WIS + 22] introduced proportionate fairness in aggregating rankings, and Chakraborty et al. [CDK + 22] developed constant-factor approximations for fair rank aggregation.

figure.head: Fair
figure.figDesc: clustering was formalized by Chierichetti et al.[CKL + 17], with subsequent work focusing on improving scalability and approximation guarantees under fairness constraints. A major bottleneck in early approaches was the cost of computing fairlet decompositions, which limited applicability to large datasets. Backurs et al. [BIO + 19] addressed this issue by proposing a near-linear time algorithm for fair k-median clustering. Their approach leverages probabilistic embeddings into hierarchically well-separated trees (HSTs) to compute (r, b)-fairlet decompositions efficiently, supporting general balance parameters and enabling scalability to massive datasets.

• t i=1 y i = S. To see this, we consider (y 1 , y 2 , . . . , y t ) after the execution of each while loop. Initially, y i is set to ⌊x i ⌋. If t i=1 y i > S, the first while loop gradually decreases t i=1 y i by 1 by decreasing a nonzero y i by 1, until t i=1 y i = y. Since min t i=1 y i = 0 and S ≥ 0, there must be an iteration where t i=1 y i = S. After this iteration, the first while loop is done. The second while loop will not be executed, and the algorithm will return (y 1 , y 2 , . . . , y t ) satisfying t i=1 y i = S. On the other hand, if t i=1 ⌊x i ⌋ < y, the first while loop is not executed. The second while loop gradually increases t i=1 y i by 1 by increasing a y i < ⌈x i ⌉ by 1, until t i=1 y i . Since S ≤ t i=1 x i ≤ t i=1 ⌈x i ⌉, there always exists some y i (≤ ⌈x i ⌉) that can be increased whenever t i=1 y t < S. Hence, there must be an iteration where t i=1 y i = S. After this iteration, the second while loop is done, and the algorithm outputs (y 1 , y 2 , . . . , y t ) such that t i=1 y i = S.
• t i=1 a i y i ≤ t i=1 a i x i . We first claim that there exists m ≤ t such that for all i < m, we have y i ≥ x i , and for all i ≥ m, we have y i ≤ x i .

If y i ≤ x i for all j, then m = 1 satisfies the claim. If there exists y i > x i , since t i=1 y i < t i=1 x i , there also exists y i < x i . Let m be the minimum index such that y m < x m , then y i ≥ x i for all j < m. Now we show that y i ≤ x i for all j ≥ m.

To see this, note that in Algorithm 1, if the second while loop is not executed, then the algorithm only decreases y i . Thus y i ≤ ⌊x i ⌋ ≤ x i for all j. The second while loop is executed only if the first while loop is not. In that case, the second while loop starts with y i = ⌊x i ⌋. If y i is increased (Algorithm 1), then y i = ⌈x i ⌉ > x i . Assume to the contrary that there exists j > m such that y j > x j . This implies that before y j is increased, t i=1 y i < S. This means that in the iteration of the for loop where i = m, we have t i=1 y i < S and by definition of m, y m < x m . It follows that y m is increased and becomes greater than x m , which is a contradiction since in the output, y m < x m .

div.head: Details of Algorithm: General Case
div.p: To describe the algorithm fair-equi we need to use a subroutine make-pdc-fair. In the subroutine make-pdc-fair, we are given a clustering I = {I 1 , I 2 , . . . ,
div.formula: I η } over a point set V . Each point v ∈ V is assigned a color from a finite set ζ = {z 1 , z 2 , . . . , z r }.
div.p: The total number of points of each color satisfies the global proportion:
div.formula: z 1 (V ) : z 2 (V ) : . . . : z r (V ) = p 1 : p 2 : . . . : p r WLOG assume p 1 > p 2 > • • • > p r .
div.p: Furthermore, for each cluster I i ∈ I, the number of points of each color z j is a multiple of p j . Recall from Chapter 3 such a clustering I is called p-divisible clustering (pdc for short).

The goal of make-pdc-fair is to construct a clustering F mpf such that for each cluster F ∈ F mpf , z 1 (F ) : z 2 (F ) : . . . : z r (F ) = p 1 : p 2 : . . . : p r Description of the subroutine make-pdc-fair: The algorithm proceeds in ⌈log 2 r⌉ iterations. At each iteration, we refine the current clustering to more closely satisfy the target color proportions. Let F 0 := I denote the initial clustering. The algorithm maintains a sequence of progressively refined clusterings:
div.formula: I = F 0 → F 1 → F 2 → . . . → F ⌈log 2 r⌉ = F mpf
div.p: In each iteration t, the algorithm enforces proportionality over small blocks of colors, where the block size increases with t. As the iterations progress, these local balancing constraints compound, eventually ensuring that the final clustering F satisfies the full global ratio p 1 : p 2 : • • • : p r within every cluster.

Description of the color blocks: We define a hierarchical merging of the color set ζ = {z 1 , z 2 , . . . , z r } over ⌈log 2 r⌉ iterations. At each iteration t, we maintain a partition of ζ into blocks {B t 1 , B t 2 , . . . , B t mt }, where each block represents a group of colors whose proportions will be jointly enforced in that round.
• Iteration 0: Initialize each color into its own singleton block:
div.formula: B 0 j = {z j } for j = 1, 2, . . . , r
div.p: • Iteration t ≥ 1: Merge adjacent blocks from the previous iteration:
div.formula: B t i = B t-1 2i-1 ∪ B t-1 2i for i = 1, 2, . . . , m t-1 2 If m t-1 is odd, then let B t ⌈m t-1 /2⌉ = B t-1 m t-1 (unchanged)
div.p: • Continue this process until the final iteration T = ⌈log 2 r⌉, where a single block B
div.formula: ⌈log 2 r⌉ 1 = ζ is formed.
div.p: At each level t, we enforce the proportionality constraints jointly over the colors in each block B t i for all clusters in the current clustering F t-1 . This recursive construction guarantees that after ⌈log 2 r⌉ rounds, the final clustering F ⌈log 2 r⌉ satisfies the global target ratio p 1 : p 2 : • • • : p r in every cluster.

div.head: Description of the algorithm fair-general:
div.p: The algorithm fair-general proceeds in two stages. First, we apply the algorithm create-pdc to the input clustering C to obtain a p-divisible clustering M. Then, we apply the algorithm make-pdc-fair on M to obtain the final fair clustering F.

6 Single-pass streaming phase: 7 foreach triple ((u, v), j, b) arriving in the stream do 8 if j ∈ J then 9 append ((u, v), b) to M 1 [j] if j ∈ K then append ((u, v), b) to M 2 [j]

Post-stream reconstruction: foreach j ∈ J do initialize a fresh union-find UF j on V foreach ((u, v), b) ∈ M 1 [j] do if b = 0 then union u and v in UF j C j ← BuildClustersFromUF(UF j ) // extract clusters from union-find Let C J ← {C j 1 , . . . , C js }.
Generate fair candidate set: F ← find-candidates(C J ) // uses α-close fair clustering algorithm
Build W from M 2 : foreach k ∈ K do initialize a fresh union-find
div.formula: UF k on V foreach ((u, v), b) ∈ M 2 [k] do if b = 0 then union u and v in UF k C k ← BuildClustersFromUF(UF k ) W ← {C k 1 , . . . , C kt }.
div.p: Select the best fair clustering on the sampled store 2:
div.formula: F ← ArgMin F ′ ∈ F C i ∈W dist(C i , F ′ ) return F
